It is recognized by all that the speed of modern warfare and the absolute necessity of immediate communications make it essential that in the case of a sea or air battle orders between major formations be given in one language only. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question also has to do with the matter of pollution. I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether or not he has received representations from one or other of the premiers of the provinces asking for the convening of a gathering of federal authorities and provincial ministers with a view to discussing the serious problem of pollution, particularly in interprovincial rivers and lakes, for the purpose of arriving at some co-operative policy to meet conditions such as prevailed recently on the North Saskatchewan river?
Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime
Minister): Yes, Mr. Speaker, there was a letter from the premier of Saskatchewan to which I replied. Having had no notice of the hon. member's question, I have not got the letter and the reply before me at the moment. As I remember it, the premier seemed to be impressed with the desirability of arrangements being made whereby the kind of situation that, unfortunately, now exists in certain parts of the eastern provinces will not be

reproduced in the western provinces in the process of their industrial development. There was a suggestion that the federal government should invite representatives of the governments of the prairie provinces to meet with it to discuss the matter.
I replied expressing the view that I thought, initially at least, it would be preferable if the premier of Saskatchewan would himself approach the premiers of Alberta and Manitoba to ascertain their views as to the desirability of that kind of meeting. I said that the federal authorities would be glad to sit in, but I felt that we should be very careful not to do anything that might carry the implication that we felt we had some sort of controlling authority over them in the determination of matters which were of provincial concern. I pointed out that at the present time we were not considering federal legislation with respect to river pollution because it would have to be legislation that would apply to the whole of Canada generally. I pointed out that what might be regarded as sufficient protection, something that would prevent the discharge of waste in running streams, would create an almost chaotic situation in the east where that was being done, as he knew, in a great many places, and that if something were to be arranged along the lines of the body that advises on the conservation of water on the eastern slope of the Rockies that was something that would be of joint provincial concern. I thought it would be preferable to approach it in a spirit of attempting to secure the kind of co-operation that would be of benefit to the whole region rather than have, at the request of one premier, something that might appear to be a summons from the federal authority to come down and discuss the manner in which they should attempt to provide against future embarrassments in that connection.
I do not remember having received any further letter from the premier of Saskatchewan since I wrote to him along those lines.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: I want to thank the Prime Minister, and ask him this question. In view of the fact this pollution problem affects rivers and lakes in all parts of our country, does he not feel that some sort of conference with all the provinces, and at least convened by the dominion, would do something to meet a situation that is becoming more serious year by year?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
I think my views coincide rather closely with those of the hon. gentleman but the most difficult problem that exists between the federal authority and the provincial authorities is to find some, if not 83276-340i
Inquiries of the Ministry permanent, attempt at a long time solution of fiscal policies. Desirable as co-operation might be in respect of the other matter, I am afraid it would be difficult to get genuine co-operation in these other matters until we have been able to arrive at something that will remove the present feelings in some parts of Canada about satisfactory fiscal arrangements between federal and provincial authorities.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps I should say a word, although there is not much I can add to the statement I made in the debate on second reading. This is the first time the Bank of Canada Act has been revised for some years. A number of technical, routine and drafting changes were made. The principal changes in policy, which I indicated in my speech on second reading, were a provision enabling the Bank of Canada to vary cash reserves of the commercial banks between 8 per cent and 12 per cent, on the conditions set out in the act. Then, there were certain changes with respect to the investment powers of the bank, and certain changes with respect to its pension fund; such provisions as an increase in the maximum remuneration to be paid to the directors, because of the fact that we now have ten provinces instead of nine, as there were when the act was brought into force. Other than that, I do not think there are any substantial proposals.
The measure was carefully studied in the committee on banking and commerce, and I must repeat what I said in connection with the Bank Act, that I appreciate warmly the careful attention given to this matter by all members in the committee in connection with both the provisions of this bill and those of the Bank Act.

speechtext:
No, I have another amendment. While I assure the minister it is just as worthy of his concurrence as the one I have just moved, I am not equally sure that it will receive his concurrence.
We have just passed an amendment dealing with the gold reserve clause, which means that the gold reserve clause is practically as if it did not exist. It is somewhat of a puzzle to me why it was left in there at all, in view of the changes in our thinking on money questions which have taken place since the passage of the Bank of Canada Act. It is left in I think as a concession to the past. For a long time, of course, it was regarded as essential. In a way it seems to me that to leave it in there is like a concession to one's grandmother: One does not smoke, perhaps, when she is around. I can explain it only as a kind of concession to good financing manners of the past. I want to make some comments because I do regard it as a matter of very considerable importance, and I hope that I may be fortunate enough, even if this amendment is not carried this morning, to interest people in it and to convince them that it is a matter of great importance.
We are all aware of course that it is only a short time since gold was considered an absolutely necessary backing to currency. I should like to read briefly from our own legislation, the Dominion Notes Act, chapter 41 of the statutes of 1927, which I believe was effective until 1933. This is what it says:
5. The Minister of Finance shall always hold as security for the redemption of dominion notes up to

and including fifty million dollars, issued and outstanding at any one time, an amount equal to not less than twenty-five per centum of the amount of such notes in gold.
Subsection 2 reads:
As security for the redemption of dominion notes issued in excess of fifty million dollars, the minister shall hold an amount in gold equal to such
excess.
And again from the Bank Act, which is chapter 12 of the Revised Statutes of 1927, section 136 reads:
Every bank which at any time holds in dominion notes less than forty per cent of the cash reserves which it has in Canada shall incur a penalty of five hundred dollars for each such offence.
Therefore we had a situation where the banks were forced to keep a large percentage of dominion notes in their hands, and where dominion notes were heavily backed in gold.
It is hard to believe that so short a time ago paper money was regarded with suspicion. We know that originally, when notes were issued, they were issued against a large percentage of actual commodities held by banks, and if a bank issued notes beyond their capacity to redeem them in commodities they did so at their peril; at any moment they might be called on to redeem the notes in a valuable commodity, usually gold. Though we seem to have passed beyond that, and many people regard that as almost prehistoric thinking, there are competent people, and by "competent people" I mean people with just as good brains as ours, who study the matter carefully, and who not only believe strongly in the gold standard, but believe that we are in great peril since we abandoned it.
I remember reading a symposium not long ago where distinguished advocates of both views were present. I was in great difficulty because when I read the views that were in favour of gold I was absolutely convinced by them, and when I read those that were against gold I was absolutely convinced by them. At the end I felt I had a kind of split personality. In any event, we have abandoned gold, and I am not standing up today to suggest that there should be any return to that at all. I am accepting the fact that we have managed money, but I am saying that managed money still leaves certain questions, and that it is very important now to inquire into the method of the management. I hope to show the committee that by the progress of events of the last twenty years, the intentions of the founders of the Bank of Canada have been entirely frustrated, and that what we have now is an entirely undemocratic and arbitrary manner of managing our currency. It is wholly in the hands of the government. I want to

emphasize that. I do not think I fully realized myself the extent to which it was true until the meetings of the banking and commerce committee. It is wholly in the hands of the government.
I shall quote answers given by the governor of the Bank of Canada and by the minister himself, which I hope will satisfy the committee that that is so, and if the committee is satisfied it is so, then I suggest that they should not brush this question aside as merely academic. Parliament at this time has no power. What I mean by that is, there is no occasion which arises, short of some crisis which will upset everything, whereby parliament has any occasion to consider the matter or to express an opinion.
It is interesting to observe that that means we have come full circle to the point when the sovereign has the full prerogative to issue money. Of course, coining was the royal prerogative for years, and it included the right of debasing the coin. In those days they did it by the open practice of clipping the coin; it was done so that you could see it. But in these days the printing press goes at it in a more refined and much less obvious way of clipping coins or debasing the currency, if we wish to do so.
It is rather interesting to find clear evidence of coin-clipping in Shakespeare. If you look at Henry IV you will find that Hotspur speaks of cracked coins being made current: in other words, bad money by legislation being made good. Many people, of course, including the advocates of gold in the symposium to which I referred, think that that is our situation today; that we have paper money with nothing behind it except the ukase of the government. I am not going to take the time of the committee to talk about the classic inflations that we all know about. But I am going to remind the committee just for a moment of the inflation in Germany in 1924 and again in the war just past. I will mention one incident which amused me, and which perhaps may amuse the committee, showing the ironies of the inflation just after the first war in Germany. This caught my eye, because it had been regarded by no less a person than Lloyd George as a very good illustration of the little ironies of life. A man in Austria left a patrimony to two sons, each of whom got an equal amount. One of them, a very sober, respectable individual, invested his share in high-grade securities. The other invested it all in wine. He drank all the wine but kept the bottles. Later on he was able to sell the bottles for more than the value of the gilt-edged securities which his pious and respectable brother had bought. That seemed
Bank of Canada Act
to tickle Mr. Lloyd George, and it is a delightful instance of being able to eat your cake, or rather drink your wine, and have it still. I mention, just as one further illustration, what has happened to the French franc. In 1913 the United States dollar was equal to 5-16 French francs. In 1954 it is equal to 350 French francs; in other words 70 times as much.
I repeat, Mr. Chairman, that what I seek to do this morning is not to argue in favour of gold. I regard it at the present time as politically unreal. Whether it will ever come back I make no predictions. But I seek to interest the committee in the present method of management of our money, to indicate it has completely subverted the intention of those who set up the Bank of Canada, to underline the fact that it has come to be the prerogative of the crown, just as it was hundreds of years ago.
It is just twenty years since the Bank of Canada was set up. The preamble to the Bank of Canada Act says that the bank is to regulate credit and currency in the best interests of the economy and the life of the nation.
And so on. Section 7 says that the governor of the bank has the direction and control of the business of the bank. I think I shall be able to satisfy the committee from answers which I shall subsequently quote, given by the governor of the bank and the Minister of Finance, that that is a thing of the past, and that in section 7, instead of saying that the governor of the bank has the direction and the control of the bank, we should say that the Minister of Finance has the direction and control of the bank. I hope that I shall be able to satisfy the committee that that is so.
The Macmillan commission, composed, as we all remember, of two competent English men, Lord Macmillan and Sir Charles Addis, of the Bank of England, Mr. Brownlee, a former premier of Alberta, Sir Thomas White and Mr. Leman, recommended two things among others in their report, which was the basis of the setting up of the bank. One was that the bank should be privately controlled and the other was that there should be a gold reserve. That was emphasized in 1934 when the bank was formed. As I said a moment ago, that has been changed. It was changed in 1936. In 1936 the bank was nationalized. I make no complaint about that whatever. I am inclined to think that private ownership of the bank, in imitation of the status of the Bank of England, which was privately owned for so many years, though of course that has been changed now, the Bank of England is now

Bank of Canada Act
nationalized

I am inclined to think that private ownership of the bank was not a very natural thing. I make no complaint whatever about its being nationalized. What I complain about is that the results which flowed from nationalization were not in the least necessary. Let me say again that the actual result, and I will come back to it later and try to establish it step by step, is that the minister can increase the money supply at his will. It is done within the four corners of the finance department. There is no occasion for public notification. It is only people who are close students of finance who have the slightest idea of what is going on.
As I have said, parliament has no say in the matter whatever. Parliament, as distinct from the government, has no more control over money increase than if parliament sat in the moon.
I am not going to take up the time of the committee to ask them to reflect on the enormous power this gives government for good or evil, a power which goes to the very basis of our lives.
Nor am I going to take up the time of the committee to dwell on inflation as it is today. We know that many people have suffered from it. I remember an occasion when a minister in this house, when high prices were criticized, said, "Well, yes, prices are high, but wages are higher." Now, that is not universally true and we all know how many people have suffered from inflation in this country. I think it was Lenin who said that the way to bring down the capitalist economy was to debauch the currency.
But despite that we have this complacency. We say it could not happen here. But in my opinion we must not think we have any kind of Divine immunity. What I want to say is that it can happen here or anywhere and we should be on our guard against it in every possible way.
Now, how has this situation come about? There are two parties concerned. First of all, there is the government. Well, I shall not repeat what we have said so often as to the increase in government power. The government has gone on taking more and more power for it is convenient and, in their view, it is businesslike to do so with as many things as possible, without coming to parliament.
We are now familiar with the phrase, "Who is to stop us?" and other things have been said in this house which I shall not repeat.
I would say this though, Mr. Chairman: I think that yesterday morning we had a new high in the disregard of this house by members of the government when serious arguments were made on an important question, 
to wit, the reform of the Senate, and when the government did not deign to say one word in reply.
We have sunk pretty low when an opposition apparently need not be answered. Indeed, the only answer was an aside which came from the other side of the house and I do not even know if it is in Hansard, to the effect that the government's answer will be given by action.
Well, there has been a long time without action and just in passing I would point out that in my opinion the fact that we were treated yesterday as people whose words were not worthy of answering registered a new low in the regard which this government has for this House of Commons to which they are responsible.

At any rate, Mr. Chairman, my feeling is that the voters have slipped into a situation

where they are interested only in the quantity of money, the quantity they have in their own pockets, and they have lost track of the quality of money. My aim this morning is to try to convince this committee that the quality of money is a most important matter. When my socialist friends talk about money for this and that 1 feel I would like to interest them in the idea of the quality of money, because if you give a man twice as many dollars which are worth less than half, then you have not done very much for him. I am through with that too, Mr. Chairman.
At the present time, as I have said, this all-important question is left to the judgment of a few men. We have respect for these men but they are not infallible and in my opinion they are not the only people who should have, on occasion, the right to express an opinion as to the soundness and validity of our currency. As it is now there is no occasion when all the other experts, and there are other experts, can express an opinion, and there is no need to call them in at all.
Let us be realistic about this. Do any of us believe that politics could never enter into the situation? Let us imagine a government not as responsible as this government considers itself to be, and let us admit that this supposed irresponsible government we are now talking about is coming on to an election. Is it very farfetched to assume that that could affect their attitude. In this connection a thoughtful comment was made to me that the prospect of the long-run value of money being determined by short-run considerations is frankly terrifying. As a matter of fact, if I were prepared to trust this power to any group of men it would not be to the cabinet exclusively. If it were possible to entrust that power to any group of men I would rather have a group consisting of, let us say, general economists, labour economists, railway economists, farm economists, businessmen, bankers, and-[DOT]

Of course, I do not suggest that that can happen. It could not happen for, of course, the government has to take the responsibility in the end; but I am utterly opposed to the present situation, which is that parliament has no part but that the government has the exclusive power. That power is exercised in private and without notice.
Bank of Canada Act
It is rather interesting to point out that in Australia they have dealt with this situation. In Canada if there is a knock-down and drag-out difference of opinion between the governor of the central bank, which was set up to regulate credit and currency, and the Minister of Finance the only recourse of the governor, as appears from the evidence before the banking and commerce committee, is to resign. Though it was not mentioned I suppose there is another course; I suppose it is possible that the governor may say, "I will not resign. I will defy you." But that is asking quite a lot.
On the other hand, in Australia in 1951, and I found this very interesting, the Central Bank Act recognized the possibility of a difference of opinion between the governor of the bank and the treasury, the institution which corresponds to our finance department, and they provided that in such an event the two views should be laid on the table of parliament so that the matter might become public and the opinion of the governor was before the people. They then had a chance of knowing what the difference was and weighing it. At the present time we in Canada may never know that there are any objections at all.

I seem to be extremely unfortunate, Mr. Chairman. I hope that perhaps what I say from now on will seem to you to be more relevant. If I am not getting on any better with anyone else in the committee than I am with you, my hopes of carrying this amendment are beginning to recede.
I now come to some of the questions and answers in the committee itself and I hope these will be considered to be relevant. If these are not relevant, I am going to have to confess that I shall have to go and try to relearn the meaning of relevance all over again. I am making the point, Mr. Chairman, that I believe it is extremely unwise that the finance department should have uncontrolled power to increase our money supply. I think you will agree that it is relevant to my amendment, which seeks to put a ceiling on the money supply. I now propose to read some of the answers I obtained in the banking and commerce committee. I asked Mr. Towers with regard to the abandonment of the gold clause in the original act. As reported at page 763 of the committee's proceedings, his reply was as follows:
It was never in effect, because it was always suspended as I recall it.
Later I asked him whether the bank now has unlimited power to create money. His answer was "yes". In answer to a later question from me as to whether there was any check on the power to issue money, as reported at page 764 Mr. Towers said this:
I referred the other day to a red light which might flash in such circumstances for instance if the governor of the central bank resigned.

I want to stress that answer. I think it is extremely important. We have now reached a point where the situation is utterly contrary to the intention of the report of the Macmillan commission and those who founded the bank, where the governor has been reduced to the position of being merely an adviser of the Department of Finance and where his answer, when asked if there is any way of controlling the issue of money, is to say, "Well, I might resign". Later on, as I shall bring to the attention of the committee, the minister fully agreed with him. He said that if the governor of the bank did not agree-1 think those were his words; I shall read them later-he thought it was his duty to resign.
In answer to a later question from me as to whether there was any check on the power to issue money Mr. Towers said:
I referred the other day to a red light which might flash . . .
Incidentally I told the governor that I thought it was a great pity if that was to be the result. I said I did not want the governor to resign. I value the governor highly, and I do not think he should be put in that position. I have already pointed out to the committee that that situation has been remedied in Australia.
As reported on the same page 764 I asked further of the governor:
In your opinion would it not be a good thing to have some kind of legislative hurdle that has to be taken before the barriers are opened beyond a certain point?
Mr. Towers replied:
I do not know of any practical way of doing it short of being on the gold standard and having provision for a minimum gold reserve.
But then he added this, Mr. Chairman, and I draw your attention particularly to it. I hope you will consider that this is relevant. He said:
The only other way in which I could think of it being accomplished would be to write into a statute that the sum total of the note and deposit liabilities of the Bank of Canada should be no greater than a sum named-an absolute amount.
Precisely my suggestion, Mr. Chairman, is put forward. I must say he did not put it forward with enthusiasm but it is put forward by the governor of the bank with this caution, which I shall now read. The governor then added:
As they are today, $2,300 million, I have forgotten the exact figure-that they should be no greater than some other amount somewhat above that, but I should think that it would be necessary to leave sufficient leeway-because parliament is not always in session-so that the damage could be done in any event, that is the damage which you fear.

I think there is a misprint there. But it is perfectly clear that the governor was saying that if there was to be any fixed limit to be put on, regard must be had for flexibility; and I would agree with that suggestion. In the committee I said to the minister that I was not wedded to 10 per cent and if he suggested, say 11 per cent, I would settle with him at once. However, I am sorry to say that he did not suggest 11 per cent.
Finally the governor of the bank said this, and I could not disagree with him. He said that I was getting into matters of policy and that the answer would have to be given by the minister. I felt that I could not quarrel with that statement. However, I also could not help feeling that the status of the governor of the bank was sadly altered from what it was in the minds of those who set up the Bank of Canada. They said that he was to be in control-with his directors, of course-of its management.
I stress what Mr. Towers said as to the possibility of just such a measure as that which I am proposing, though with the caution of flexibility which I accept. After all, the crisis is not going to come on us like an atomic bomb. If there is a money crisis there will be days, perhaps weeks and possibly months when the situation is developing. As we all know from our experience of four years ago, parliament can be called together in two or three days, or inside a week anyway.
I now come to the evidence of Mr. Abbott. As reported at page 1347 of the proceedings of the banking and commerce committee 1 recounted to him what I had asked Mr. Towers and in reply he said:
I suppose, Mr. Macdonnell, what you are asking me to comment upon is whether there should be some definite limitations in the Bank of Canada Act or the Currency Act or both on the powers of the central bank with respect to the issue of currency; as I take it you are not suggesting we should now return to a full-fledged gold standard?

I would prefer to allow the matter-and this is only my personal view-to remain as it is at the present time because I do not know of any better alternative.
Bank of Canada Act
Again I asked this question:
But would you not agree that with our so-called irresponsible government it might be useful to have a situation arise where the public is put on notice?
To that question Mr. Abbott replied as reported at page 1348 of the proceedings:
I agree with Mr. Towers: I must say if the Minister of Finance and thereby the government of the day suggested a policy which the central bank could not go along with I think the governor of the central bank should give the warning signal by resigning. I think it would be his duty to do it, but I do not believe it is either desirable, or feasible perhaps, to spell that out by legislation. That is really the only way I can answer your question.
I asked again. I was very persistent, although I do not think I was irrelevant. I said:
. . . are you satisfied with the wide-open situation where there is no limit of any kind on the power to increase the money supply.
The minister replied:
I know of no other way. Yes, I am satisfied with the present situation.
The minister was frank and forthright, as he always is. He did not even tell me he would give the matter his consideration, as he sometimes does. He says:	Leave it to
parliament and to the people. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that that is not an answer which the minister's biographer will put in the forefront of his biography.

I think it is a very unrealistic answer. We are told that we control the C.B.C. because we get a report from them once a year, and we all know how effective that is. 1 felt that the minister's answer was vague and unsatisfactory. He said there might be circumstances which would make this unwise. But the only circumstance that he mentioned, as far as I recall, was the possibility of hoarding. I do not think that has ever been a very great danger in this country, but I am ready to admit, and I have said all along, that I do not regard my ideas on this matter as necessarily the only way out. I say that parliament should somehow or other be introduced into the picture, and if my suggestion is not the best then let us have a better way. I say again that the minister, without any notice to the public, can go ahead and increase the money supply.
1 have already put it to the committee that the original Bank Act contemplated private ownership and reserves and that both of these were changed. I am making no comment on the change but I am drawing the attention of the committee to the frank expression given by Mr. Dunning in 1936 when the change was made which points out ever

Bank of Canada Act
so clearly what was contemplated and makes it clear that what was contemplated was a complete reversal, I submit, of what was indicated when the central bank act had been passed two years before. I quote from what Mr. Dunning said on June 1, 1936, as found at page 3260 of Hansard:
The matter of public ownership is in my opinion much less important than that of government control. If we study the constitution of central banks from this aspect, we shall find ample precedent for the attempt which we are making to give the government adequate control over the Bank of Canada.
In 1934 Mr. King had also used somewhat similar words, though he spoke of the public opinion of the nation. I will read his words:
There are times when it is necessary and vital that every institution in the land should be subject to the public opinion of the nation-
Could I have a better endorsement of what I am arguing? All I am arguing is that there are times when public opinion should express itself. Mr. King continued:
-and this is always the case when it is expressed in a constitutional way in parliament.
I submit again that it is this parliamentary control that I am seeking to have re-established. My proposal is not very dramatic or drastic. If it were, perhaps it might have more chance. However, it is not unprecedented. There is a measure of control at any rate in the United Kingdom over the fiduciary note issue. There is a measure of control, as I pointed out in the committee, in the United States and, what is also important, there is the frankest public discussion between the federal reserve bank and the treasury of the United States on matters of policy.
There is nothing of the kind here. The governor of the bank expresses his views in the four corners of the Department of Finance and then he is through. What would be the effect of my amendment? Merely that when we get to a certain point the people of Canada would be entitled to have a look at the position of their currency. That is all I am advocating. There is no disrespect to the finance department in saying that they are not infallible. The minister would be the first one to admit it. The minister says that he does not believe we can by legislation protect either ourselves or our descendants against our follies. I would agree with that of course, but that seems to be no answer to the suggestion that the people should be allowed at a certain point to have a look at their own affairs.

Mr. Chairman, I suppose members of all political parties who have been members of the banking and commerce committee have met the fate that I and my colleagues in this group who were members of that committee have met of late,

that whenever we mention the more recondite details of banking we are just not allowed to discuss them. So you will have to forgive the hon. member for Greenwood and myself if we have this last final scamper over the peaks of high finance. I am grateful to the hon. member for Greenwood for giving us this opportunity but I must add that I cannot agree with the case that he has put before us. His case is that there should be some legal limit to the expansion of our total money supply. On the face of it that seems reasonable until we come to examine the mechanics by which our total money supply is increased or decreased. When we do that I do not see how we can escape the conclusion that this proposal is in the first place impractical and, in the second place, if it were practical, it is quite unnecessary.
So far as its impracticality is concerned, I would suggest that it is almost impossible for anyone to make an estimate, even within the fair latitude that the hon. member for Greenwood has suggested, of the necessities for any one particular period. I went to the trouble of getting figures for the total money supply in every year from 1945 until March of this year which I think will illustrate the point fairly well. You will recall, Mr. Chairman, that the hon. member for Greenwood pointed out that we went through quite a serious inflationary period in that period of years, and he suggested that if we had had this control we might perhaps have avoided some of the more unpleasant features of that inflationary period.

I am sorry if I am imputing something to him, but I gathered that was the idea, that we had a warning in this post-war period of the dangers of not having control over our total money supply. In 1945 our total monetary supply was $5,905 million. The following year it was $6,852 million, an increase of about 17 per cent; that is in the immediate postwar year.
Now, here is the significant part. From that time forward our increase each year has been very much less than that. The following year it was some 3 per cent; between 1947-48, it was about a 10 per cent increase. Then it dropped between 1948-49 to a 5 per cent increase; 1949-50 it became about a 15 per cent increase. The following year there was only a fraction of 1 per cent increase, and the following year again it jumped to an 8 per cent increase, and then the following year it was down to almost nil, practically no

difference. In 1952 it was $9,302 million and in 1953, $9,345 million. Up to March of this year it has increased slightly over 1 per cent over the corresponding period last year.
I suggest, therefore, even if we wished to do so it would be very difficult indeed to place any really effective limit to which we could point. I would suggest this. For instance, who could tell-certainly not the Minister of Finance although he might perhaps have warnings before some of us-whether or not we were going to have a vast increase in investment in Canada from abroad? If we did, it would immediately necessitate a vast increase in our total monetary supply. In fact, one could relate many of these increases to just that factor. I suggest it is, in the first place, an impractical suggestion.
Then, I come to the next point, and that is as to whether or not it is necessary to do so. On the face of it, as I say, it does seem rather frightening, shall we say, when we look across the aisle to realize that at any moment the Minister of Finance may be replaced by some fallible creature. Then, where shall we be? I believe that we are giving the Minister of Finance or his office credit for rather more power than it actually possesses.

I have an idea there is far more automatism, shall I say, in this process than we readily understand or are prepared to admit. I wish I had the exact words of Mr. Towers on this point in the banking and commerce committee, but perhaps those who were there will agree that I am recalling them correctly. When we were engaged in a discussion of this point, I asked him if he would agree that from a certain point of view it would be correct to say that our total money supply was nothing more than a reflection of our economic activity at any particular period. Mr. Towers agreed that that was a point of view that could be sustained. I think it is the actual fact of the situation. I believe the money supply of the country will depend, in the final analysis, on the level of investment, either internally by government action or from abroad by foreign action, and that in order to cope with that situation the Bank of Canada will almost automatically have to increase our total money supply.
I would suggest too that there is probably nothing better calculated to undermine public confidence in our monetary system than to periodically have parliament summoned into a special session to increase the total money supply, or even every session to have the Minister of Finance come to us, perhaps with some urgency, and tell us that before the

Bank of Canada Act
current week or month were out we had to take steps to increase the total money supply. This would bring to the minds of people not accustomed to dealing with these ideas some very disquieting thoughts. Many of them would hark back to the old days of inflation of currency by the printing press or even perhaps back farther to the methods described by the hon. member for Greenwood, the debasement of actual currency. I am very much afraid we would have many people stuffing currency into mattresses and into socks, and that would not have a very desirable effect upon the economy.
I would conclude, Mr. Chairman, by suggesting to the hon. member for Greenwood that even the most lighthearted government or even the most responsible government would have the greatest difficulty in actually inflating our total money supply beyond the level of our real economic activity no matter how much they might want to do it. Let us consider how they might go about it. We will suppose the present Minister of Finance, through some tragic accident, had suddenly gone mad and decided he was going to inflate the monetary supply. He was going to flood us with dollar bills and $10 bills. He issues an order to the Bank of Canada to do that. They pile them up, wherever the Bank of Canada does pile them up, or wherever it is they have them stacked up, knee high. Then, the problem arises, how are we going to infuse these bills into our economic system, because they will not inflate the monetary supply sitting there. These bills can only be infused into the economy by means of economic activity that is engaged in actual production of goods and services. So long as it is limited in that way, then I feel the danger of runaway inflation is something we do not need to seriously consider.

If that is the case, then I think it is incumbent upon the hon. member for Greenwood to tell us exactly what it is he does mean. It is certain that what he has been trying to introduce into our money policy is some mechanism that will seriously restrict the amount of money that is going to be in use in the Dominion of Canada; that is the very purpose of the amendment which he introduced today. It is a modified gold standard, if he does not call it that.
In the questioning that took place in the committee, I noticed my hon. friend and his colleagues, whenever it was possible, did question very closely about the necessity of having some sort of reserve that would afford automatic control of the money supply. Well, of course, that is nothing more or less than perhaps a modification of the straight and rigid gold standard. Let me just say this, that the gold standard could not work in Canada today without forcing the government to abandon all those things they have introduced into the economy for the purpose of stabilizing it. They would have to throw unemployment insurance, family allowances and all that sort of thing away, because a gold standard simply cannot work unless there is considerable fluctuation in internal price levels, as compared with external price levels, so that it would encourage the movement into or out of the country, as the case might be, of quantities of gold. It is just impossible.
The only alternative is a managed money system, which this country has adopted and which, I think, is infinitely superior to a gold standard in its effects upon the economy and welfare of the people generally. And so, anything that even approximately approaches a gold standard I must oppose at once.
Now, in his talk the hon. member for Greenwood-and I give him credit for being honest in his convictions, of course; I am prepared to take what he says as being

exactly what he feels and thinks-the hon. member for Greenwood complains about inflation, and he cited the situation that has developed in Canada.
Well, I notice that he very carefully avoided saying anything about deflation-not one single word did he say. But I point out to members of the House of Commons that deflation can be and often is more devastating to the country as a whole, and to the welfare of the people, than inflation. I have heard nothing from him or from his colleagues in the committee to suggest that they have the means whereby they can prevent devastating deflation. As a matter of fact, it seems to me the only things they have advocated are those things which would encourage a deflationary trend and, so far as I am concerned, I do not like that sort of thing. On the one hand, I do not want inflation; but, equally, I do not want deflation. I think we ought to be trying to find some mechanism which will prevent any undue inflation or deflation, either of which militates against the best interests of the people of the country.
What I am trying to discover, as we sail through these uncharted seas, is a means whereby we can accomplish this double purpose. The thing I think we should be trying to do is to adopt that type of government policy which will reduce to an irreducible minimum inflationary forces on the one hand and deflationary forces on the other, because both of them are devastating.
In the course of his address the hon. member for Greenwood suggested that perhaps it is unwise to leave the determination of the amount of money in the country to the Minister of Finance and his colleagues. He suggested that perhaps it would be wise to have a group of people representing economists in agriculture, economists in business and economists in law-and all that sort of thing.

Well, perhaps so. But let me suggest to the hon. member for Greenwood that we have pretty much that sort of thing now, in the set-up of the Bank of Canada. They have a great number of very capable economists, businessmen and financiers with whom they collaborate in determining what the policy shall be at any given time, and to meet such circumstances as might arise. I am sure their advice and counsel is taken very seriously.
Bank of Canada Act
So far as I can see, the set-up is almost essentially what the hon. member has suggested. In the course of the years we have made a suggestion at various times for the setting up of a permanent monetary commission composed of representatives of the Bank of Canada, the chartered banks, the Department of Finance, agriculture, labour, and business generally throughout the country. Perhaps it might be an expansion of the board of the Bank of Canada, which would meet regularly to consider all of these questions with regard to the financial and monetary policy of the country. Such a permanent monetary commission in our view should be made responsible directly to the representatives of the people in the House of Commons much as the Auditor General is today, so that periodically they could be called before a committee of the House of Commons and hon. members could be kept informed.
It seems to me that a permanent monetary commission of that sort might be the answer to this whole dilemma. I can understand the concern of the hon. member for Greenwood about having the parliament of Canada consulted frequently about the monetary policy of the country, and the results of policies which have been in effect. As I say, I can understand his concern in that regard; and I think perhaps the best way of meeting it would be to have the type of permanent monetary commission I have suggested, a body which would be responsible to the House of Commons, just as the Auditor General is responsible. We could get from that commission independent reports, and periodically it could give evidence before us. In that way we could keep our finger on this matter.
The commission could be charged with the overseership of policy drafted and set up by the House of Commons; and the overseership and management by that commission could include this very important point, which I think is of such tremendous importance to the people of Canada.
There are two sets of figures available. There is the set of figures representing the production of the country available to be moved and used. There is also the set of figures available showing us month after month the total money supply. Well, most certainly it seems to me that the duties of a monetary commission might be to gear the two sets of figures together, and by so doing it would be possible for them to determine, with more or less accuracy, what the financial and monetary policy of the country is doing. Perhaps they could advise the Bank of Canada and the Minister of Finance about

Bank of Canada Act
what ought to be done to meet the situation developing in the country in months ahead.
Now, that sort of thing is practicable, I believe. I am not at any time suggesting that it is possible for a small group of men to decide how much money this country needs. I think the only way that can be done is to leave it to the vast number of entrepreneurs, the producers, the business people and the like, who go to the chartered banks in the regular course of business and arrange for loans for production purposes and by the means now used determine pretty closely the money supply.
But there is another feature of it which I think has to be considered, and that is this, that there are times in this country, as there are in every other country which operates under a financial system such as ours, where, especially in peacetime, surpluses of goods and services do accumulate, and cannot be moved.
Now, if we are to leave the problem of the distribution of those unsaleable surpluses so that it will regulate itself-well, I say we just never would have them distributed, and we may go into a devastating recession or depression.
Our suggestion in those circumstances has been and still remains that the government should provide itself with a mechanism under which purchasing power can be obtained from the only source of new purchasing power, the Bank of Canada, in limited quantity. Limit it to that amount of goods and services which need to be distributed in a country-goods and services which are clearly there and which can be seen and determined quite simply. And simply see to it that that purchasing power is obtained interest free from the Bank of Canada and be used by injecting it directly into the hands of the ultimate consumers so they can thrust it quickly into effective demand to buy the goods off the market and thus themselves set the wheels of industry in motion and help to keep the plants going. That is the proposition that has been made. My hon. friend's amendment would not take care of that at all. My hon. friend's amendment would do the opposite. It would limit severely the amount of money that could be in use at any given time- It is not unreasonable to gear the money supply to the productive capacity of our country. Let the capacity demand decide what the money supply shall be.
If we have in a given period of time an increase of 10 per cent in our production in the country, is it not reasonable to suppose that we are going to need a considerable increase, perhaps up to a maximum

of 10 per cent, in the money supply so as to be able to distribute the goods? If there is a 3 per cent increase in productive capacity in our country at any given period, is it unreasonable to suppose that we shall need perhaps a maximum of 3 per cent increase in the money supply? Why, certainly any reasonable person would say, that is what we need. But if we tie ourselves to an amendment of this kind, we are not in a position at any time to increase the money supply sufficient to meet the needs of an increased productive capacity.
I think it is high time that we began to take a look at the irresponsibles. My hon. friend has talked a whole lot about irresponsible governments. I noticed that on the various occasions he looked right straight across at the Social Credit members of the committee. I would rather he would get up and say, what I am trying to provide against is the irresponsible Social Credit bunch getting in and debasing our currency. Instead of that he skirts around and talks in a sort of whisper about irresponsible governments. I like my hon. friend; I am not angry with him at all; but I should like to point out that Social Crediters have been responsible in their administration of affairs. If he can find a better administration of financial affairs than we get in Alberta where we have dominated for 20 years, then I should like him to show us.

Mr. Chairman, this has been a most interesting debate this morning, and I am very greatly indebted to all hon. members who have taken part in it. It has been raised by the hon. member for Greenwood proposing the amendment which he did in the banking and commerce committee and which in effect of course is to insert a statutory limitation on the power of the Bank of Canada to expand currency and credit. He is suggesting that that be inserted in section 23 of the Bank of Canada Act. In substance he is substituting for the old limitation that the note and deposit liabilities of the Bank of Canada should not exceed four times the amount of its gold reserves, another limitation that they should not exceed the amount at which they stand when the bill receives royal assent plus 10 per cent.. I indicated to the banking and commerce committee that I could not accept such an amendment.
Since September of 1939 we have had of course what is commonly known as a managed currency.

speechtext: Did it begin only then?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MANAGEMENT, EXCHANGE, TO PERMIT SHORT TERM LOANS ON INSURED MORTGAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
That is my recollection; it may have been before that but certainly since September, 1939, we have had what is commonly known as a managed currency, and I think that the provisions of this section of the Bank of Canada Act have been suspended since that time.
It is a matter of opinion whether we should have an automatic limitation on the expansion of currency and credit, such as existed in the Bank of Canada Act before the war, by reason of the gold provision or such as is suggested by my hon. friend in his amendment today.
I am indebted to the hon. member for Nanaimo for the very concise exposition which he gave to the committee of the way in which a managed currency operates so far as the expansion of currency and credit is concerned. I must confess that I am in large measure in agreement with the views which he expressed as to both the impracticability and the undesirability of the amendment which has been suggested by the hon. member for Greenwood. I personally believe that it would be extremely unwise to insert this element of rigidity into the Bank of Canada Act. My friend has given me credit and has given the government credit for a great deal more power than we possess in this respect. He has suggested that the governor of the Bank of Canada, or the management of the Bank of Canada-I think he said the governor of the Bank of Canada-is a captive. If T may paraphrase Winston Churchill's statement, all I can say is he is some captive.
Bank of Canada Act
The governor and the management of the Bank of Canada have certain clearly defined responsibilities and certain clearly defined rights under the Bank of Canada Act. It is open of course to parliament at any time to change those rights and responsibilities but with the exception of this amendment, my hon. friend has suggested no change in that respect. The government as such, the Minister of Finance as such, has no control over the note issue of the Bank of Canada. That is exclusively within the control of the bank itself. So far as the expansion of credit of the bank is concerned, it is true, as I indicated to the banking and commerce committee, that if the government indulged over a period of time in deficit financing and issued securities, either short or long term, which were purchased by the Bank of Canada, it would constitute a substantial expansion of credit. But I would remind my hon. friend that the government cannot borrow at all on short or long term except in virtue of authorization by this house. That should always be remembered. Therefore there is in fact a very real measure of parliamentary control, a complete measure of parliamentary control over the final result.
He has made the point that the public should know, the people of Canada should know, what is going on. I entirely agree with him, but I must confess that when you look at the weekly statements of the Bank of Canada, which are very concise statements, they indicate exactly the extent and character of the deposit and other liabilities of the Bank of Canada and the assets which the bank has. These are published in the press of this country each week, and they are compared with the figures of the week before. Now, anybody who has learned to read can look at those figures and understand what they mean. Mr. Chairman, before this amendment is put to a vote I should like to give a little attention to the matter of responsibility, as it applies particularly to the Conservative party.
We all understand that there were conditions imposed upon the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett which under the circumstances were probably impossible for him to control. But let us just find out whether Mr. Bennett and the Conservatives in power in 1930 were able to do anything at all to prevent vast sums of money from being taken out of circulation in Canada with the resulting destruction of industry and the prosperity of the nation.
The Hon. C. H. Cahan, speaking on November 13, 1933, and I am speaking entirely here from memory, said that over $900 million had been withdrawn from circulation in Canada since the beginning of the depression.
Now, following up what the hon. member for Peace River said, I would like to hear the hon. member for Greenwood tell us what he would have done to keep that $900 million from being taken out of circulation, or to put it back into circulation once it had been taken out.
There you have a real job and I will warrant that the hon. member for Greenwood would not be able to say now what he would do except perhaps that he would talk to us beautifully as he so often does.
Let me turn to another matter. The hon. member spoke about inflation. No doubt he had in mind the tremendous increase in prices which has resulted in this country since 1946. That so-called inflation, which it really was not, was a deliberate rise in price which came about as the result of the Conservatives in 1945-46 demanding that controls be removed before the production of this country had reached a level which would justify the removal of controls. The government, which had held the price structure in Canada at an astonishingly stable level, with Donald Gordon in charge, was obliged by pressure from the Conservatives to remove these controls and so the price structure went skyrocketing, even although we were living in peacetime.

It is not nearly as much of a compliment as my hon. friend thinks it is. Hon. members will recall that the first move in this price rise, which so many people mistakenly called inflation, was that the steel companies of Canada, with the consent of the government, advanced their price for steel by $5 per ton.
Perhaps the hon. member for Greenwood can tell me whether that is or is not a fact. Now, just as soon as that increase of $5 per ton in steel was granted, then the steel workers demanded at once that they be given a share of the money which the steel companies made as a result of that advance in price. The result was that they struck for 82 days and finally obtained that concession.
Now, what did these two moves bring about in the Canadian economy? The price of steel, as everyone knows-

I think so too, Mr. Chairman, and that is exactly what I propose to do. The hon. member was talking about responsibility and I was just going to point out that that increase in the price of steel resulted in an increase in the cost of production in respect of practically everything else throughout the nation's industry. The increase in the steel workers' pay resulted finally in an increase in the charge structure in every industry in the nation, and the two together jacked up prices point after point to the extent where they are still rising at the present time. In addition to that, taxation was being increased at the same time. If you want irresponsibility you have it personified in the men of the Conservative party who rose and demanded the removal of price controls. For them to stand up now, despite the havoc which resulted in the Canadian economy by reason of their imprudent demand for the removal of price control, and call the resultant price rise inflation is for them to provide abundant evidence that they just do not know what they are talking about any time they speak.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I have dealt with the general aspects of the matter and I would now like to say a word or two more about responsibility. There is plenty more to be

said along this line. The hon. member for Peace River referred to the government of Alberta as an instance of responsible government. Therein the Social Credit government, never mind how they did it, which, granted it had to operate in accordance with methods of orthodox finance-and look how magnificently they did it-took a debt of $167 million, which looked impossible to deal with, and completely liquidated it. Perhaps they have not actually liquidated it completely, but at least they now have the money with which to deal with it. They now have in addition a vast amount of money saved up-and that has never been done before in the history of the Dominion of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, when I closed there was a whole collection of members across the way on the Liberal side who were clamouring for me to let them ask questions. I told them that I would be quite happy to stay here until midnight to answer their questions if they brought them along; but they have not come forth; so I presume we might as well treat their questions as being all answered.
I was dealing briefly with the question of responsibility in government. I have no desire to spend any great amount of time on it, but there were cries from various parts of the house to the effect that it was Alberta's oil which had done wonders in reforming conditions in Alberta not Alberta's Social Credit government. I just wish to give one set of figures and then I propose to go on with another aspect of the argument of the hon. member for Greenwood. Official figures indicate that on March 31, 1936, Alberta's net funded debt and guarantees amounted to $148,613,000 and that on March 31, 1948, the amount was only $121,504,000. In other words $27,109,000 had been paid by Alberta before oil in considerable amount began to come in. The real revenue from oil began to come in with the discovery of the great Leduc field in 1947. We will now leave that matter. Any time my good friends want to ask questions about Alberta, let them just come around and if they let me know beforehand we will have a good time.
The hon. member for Greenwood, in his argument in support of his position, referred to Germany as a horrible example of what starts in case the gold standard is not rigidly adhered to. Inasmuch as this is a new parliament I think we might as well have a sort of showdown on this German question. It is well to remember a thing which men like the hon. member for Greenwood apparently never take the trouble to find out, namely that Germany, previous to her famous inflation, had fought a long and exhausting war for four years and that Germany was defeated. That means that she was left at the mercy of those who had won. Any government that tries to keep its money somewhere near stable under conditions like that will experience plenty of trouble. I think the Minister of Finance will be the first man to testify to that truth. He knows how careful he has to be to keep matters under control with a very strong government, a very strong country and a very strong people in Canada.
At the close of that war there was owed by the German government a debt of 147 billion gold marks. May I draw the attention of the hon. member for Greenwood to the fact that they were gold marks, not paper
5388	HOUSE OF
Bank of Canada Act
marks? Of this debt, 58 billion was floating debt and 89 billion was funded debt. The interest on that money had to be paid every year. The total taxation which the government could raise in Germany amounted to just enough to take care of one-tenth of the floating debt alone. Let me ask the hon. member for Greenwood this question. After his careful studies of finance, of which I hope he makes a great many, just what would he have done if he had been in charge of the German government in those years? Would he have permitted default on the debt and the interest on the debt? If he was going to get the moneys to pay the debt, where would he have got the money? It might be said that he would float a loan amongst German people. But the German people had no money. Let him face that problem. I hope he does so.
What happened to Germany was much worse than what I have already pictured. The London conference forced Germany to pay one billion gold marks in August, 1921, 362 million gold marks in March, 1922 and 254 million gold marks in August, 1922. For a country that had been on a strict gold standard-so strict a gold standard that they had 60 per cent as much gold as they had notes in circulation at the opening of the war-that export of gold would have been enough to destroy utterly the confidence of the people both within the country and outside of it.
In order to meet the situation the government borrowed from the Reichsbank money to pay on the debt. Let it be remembered that this was not government-issued money. It was good bank money issued by the German Reichsbank to pay on the debt. Hon. members Who wish to check any of these figures may do so by asking for a fine book which is to be found in our library, or it used to be before the fire-called "The Story of Money" by Sir Norman Angell, published in 1929. In it they will find a chapter on German inflation which will be very enlightening and will support everything I am saying here now.
Terrible losses were sustained by Germany. In the first place her colonies were swept away. In the next place her merchant marine was swept away. In the next place much of her trade was swept away. In the next place the extremely rich Ruhr-Lorraine-Luxem-bourg industrial unit in Germany was taken away or disrupted.

I am just endeavouring to show the absolute weakness of the hon. member's position. His arguments are just not valid at all. He had a hodge-podge of sayings that are commonly accepted as true coin but they have no meaning at all when one examines into them.
I was going on with the German situation, Mr. Chairman. The treaty of peace disrupted the valuable Ruhr-Lorraine-Luxem-bourg industrial unit in Germany which meant that it destroyed between 11 per cent and 15 per cent of Germany's productive capacity. The hon. member for Greenwood made a revealing remark at one time. He said that inflation was having too many dollars chasing too few goods. In Germany you will notice that all the things I have mentioned up to the present time would affect Germany's ability to produce goods, at the same time leaving money out in circulation. Thus the stage was set for serious inflation. The treaty of peace did worse than that or it did more. It forced Germany to deliver immense amounts of railway cars, locomotives, chemicals, dyes, coke, coal and agricultural products, just the very things that Germany needed as goods to support her money.
Those things being considered, I think everyone will grant that for the hon. member to bring in the German inflation situation, in order to illustrate his case or to fortify it, was not for him to manifest the best of judgment.
I thank you for your courtesy, Mr. Chairman.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. M. Benidickson (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CERTAIN ACTS TO PRESCRIBE PENSION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I stated the other day when the resolution on this bill was being considered, it is designed to prescribe the pension provisions for, and the manner in which those pension provisions are to apply to, persons transferring their employment from the public service to a number of crown corporations. The same provisions will affect the employees of boards, commissions and other corporations who contribute under the Public Service Superannuation Act should they become employees of those crown corporations to which this bill applies.
Hitherto in accordance with the provisions of the Government Companies Operation Act, as well as of a number of other acts establishing crown companies, a civil servant who had been contributing to the superannuation account under the Civil Service Superannuation Act could continue to be a contributor and enjoy all the benefits of the superannuation act, if he left his employment in the civil service, and became an employee of one of these crown companies. It is believed that this policy was introduced to encourage the transfer of key personnel from the civil service at the time of the establishment of a crown company. As a rule it would be some time before the company would have a pension plan of its own and so these civil servants, many with several years to their credit under the superannuation act, would otherwise be transferring from an employment with a first-class pension plan to one with none at all.
While such a provision was recognized as essential at a time when a company was set

up, the need for it gradually disappears when a company becomes well established and has a good pension plan of its own. Up to the present those civil servants who have benefited in this way on becoming employees of crown companies would at least have been permanent civil servants and would normally have several years of service to their credit. Thus the retention of this right to remain under the Civil Service Superannuation Act would not be regarded as providing very many undeserved benefits up until now.
With the coming into force of the Public Service Superannuation Act on January 1 of this year, the circumstances just described are quite different. If these provisions were to be retained in these other acts it would then be possible for a person with just over a year's employment in a temporary position to transfer to a crown company and carry with him full rights under the superannuation act because he had become a contributor to the superannuation account after this one year of employment. Since an employee who transferred to one of these crown companies would transfer because it was to his advantage to do so, it is unreasonable that he should carry with him the generally greater benefits of the public service pension plan. In addition he would have the other advantages of his new position and be relatively better off than both his former and new fellow employees.
I mentioned at the resolution stage the crown corporations with pension plans of their own to which this act will apply. These are the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, the Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation, Canadian Arsenals Limited, Polymer Corporation Limited and Eldorado Mining and Refining Limited, under whose pension plan employees of Eldorado Aviation Limited and of Northern Transportation Company Limited come. As I pointed out earlier, the acts relating to the pension plans of these crown companies contain provisions regarding the continuation of transferred employees as contributors to the superannuation account.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CERTAIN ACTS TO PRESCRIBE PENSION PROVISIONS
speechtext: Of the crown companies?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CERTAIN ACTS TO PRESCRIBE PENSION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
The acts that are now being amended have hitherto contained a provision under which a person could continue under the superannuation act. Because of its close relation with the Public Service Superannuation Act it is intended that this new act will have effect from January 1 of this year because that is the day on which that act came into force. It will not affect those civil servants who became employees of crown companies before that date and 83276-341
Crown Corporations
continued to be contributors under the superannuation act. They will continue on as before.
Hon. members will recall that the new Public Service Superannuation Act provides for reciprocal transfer agreements between the government and any of these crown companies where, on the transfer of both employer and employee contributions as well as of interest on these contributions from one pension fund to the other, the employee's full service credit under his former pension plan will be transferred to his new pension plan. This would be done only if the employee agrees and where a reciprocal transfer agreement has been concluded. Some discussion has already taken place with certain of the crown corporations with a view to entering into these agreements as provided in that act.
Thus a contributor under the superannuation act who, before the age of 60, transfers his employment to one of these crown companies which is not under that act will have the choice of at least a return of his contributions or a deferred annuity related to his service up to that time and commencing at the age of 60. If there is a reciprocal transfer agreement with this crown company, that employee would have the third choice open to him of having his pensionable service transferred to his credit under the pension plan of his new employer.
In addition to the acts relating to these corporations, the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority Act is also amended in this bill so far as the pension provisions are concerned. As hon. members are aware, the St. Lawrence seaway authority has not yet been established and it is not known, therefore, what type of pension plan it will have. This bill makes it possible for the authority to be added to schedule "A" of the Public Service Superannuation Act whereby its employees would be contributors under that act. As an alternative, should it be decided to set up a pension plan of its own, this bill provides that persons who are contributors under the Public Service Superannuation Act and who become employees of the authority will continue to be contributors under that act until the authority's own pension plan is established. At that time provisions similar to those described above for these other crown companies covered by this bill will apply to those contributors.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CERTAIN ACTS TO PRESCRIBE PENSION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when we were on the resolution stage with respect to this legislation I indicated our wholehearted support of the principle with which this legislation deals. As I understand it, the government's desire is that as between the public service and crown corporations there should be transferability of pension rights. From what the parliamentary assistant said just now I understand that the government does not wish it to go too far; it does not wish it to go to the extent of an employee getting a double advantage in terms of pension rights because he transfers from one type of government employment to another. Obviously one can have no quarrel with that aspect of the legislation.
I do wish to say once again that we support wholeheartedly the underlying principle of this legislation, namely, that when employees transfer from one type of government employment to another it should be possible for them to carry with them the pensionable service or the pension rights which they have earned.
As I indicated the other day, and therefore I shall only refer to it in passing now, we think this is a principle that should be extended even wider. The parliamentary assistant has indicated that at one stage, in order to induce people to leave the public service for employment in crown corporations, it was necessary to do something about the pension situation. That feature applies not only as between public service and crown corporation employment, but it applies as well to a great many people at all levels of employment.
As I said the other day, there are people who are frozen to their jobs because they cannot carry their pension rights with them. There are others who are effectively denied entry into certain types of employment because their age is such they cannot become participants in a particular pension plan. If such persons were able to carry with them the pension rights that they had built up in the past that problem could be solved. I rise, therefore, Mr. Speaker, to express the hope that the government, as a matter of public policy, will give further study to this whole question and will try to draft legislation that will extend this principle on a broader basis, so that our people generally

will be able to take their pension rights with them when they transfer not only from public service to crown corporations but when they transfer from private industry to public service or vice versa, or even when they transfer from one private industry to another. As I indicated the other day, this is something that is sorely needed in respect of pension plans throughout the country generally, and I hope that we will yet see an extension of the basic principle underlying this legislation until it includes all our people.
