speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 393, to amend the Atomic Energy Control Act.

He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of the proposed amendments to the Atomic Energy Control Act of 1946 is to establish administrative machinery and procedures which will better meet the requirements of the present and future program in atomic energy. The program has passed through two stages, and is now entering upon a third.
The first stage began in 1942 with Canada's decision to join with the governments of the United States and the United Kingdom in the effort to produce an atomic bomb. Canada's contribution was twofold. First, we supplied uranium-the raw material of the bomb-from the deposits at Port Radium in the Northwest Territories. This mining operation, initially under the direction of a private company, was transferred to a crown company, Eldorado Mining and Refining Limited, in January, 1944. Second, we made available the facilities of the national research council, and in particular the services of a group of brilliant scientists on its staff. These men in association with British and European scientists undertook to find a method of producing plutonium, the fissionable material which is one of the prime ingredients of the atomic bomb. As a result of this research it became possible to design and construct a reactor at Chalk River using heavy water as the moderator and natural uranium as the fuel. This project was under the direction of the national research council. While the reactor was primarily a research tool, much of the information obtained in its design and operation has been of great value to the military program. This first stage in the atomic energy program came to a close with the end of the war.
There was a period between the end of the war and late 1946 when some hope existed that a way might be found of eliminating, or at least controlling, the use of atomic weapons. In this connection the house will recall Canada's participation in the international conference on atomic energy which was held under the auspices of the United Nations. It was not thought desirable during the period of these discussions that any change should be made in the Canadian program in either the research or the raw materials fields. When it became apparent that an international agreement could not be reached consideration had to be given to the future direction of the two phases of the Canadian program, and to the best method of administering that program. This was the beginning of the second stage.
In the raw materials field the way was clear. It was decided that Canada should
Atomic Energy Control Act continue to supply uranium for the production of atomic bombs from existing sources of supply and, moreover, that we should seek to increase the sources of supply. Similar policies were adopted by the governments of the United States and the United Kingdom. This involved, in the first instance, an expansion of the production capacity at the Port Radium mine, and an expansion of Eldorado's exploration activity. It also involved the participation of the prospector and the mining industry. The house will recall that in March, 1948 I announced that a price schedule had been established for uranium ores and concentrates which was guaranteed until March 31, 1955. I also announced that Eldorado had been designated as the procurement agent for all uranium ores and concentrates produced in Canada. I have made further announcements from time to time relating to changes in the price schedule and the duration of the guarantee. The current price schedule has been guaranteed until March 31, 1962.
In considering the post-war objectives of the Chalk River project the government was influenced largely by the fact that the NRX reactor had proved to be the most efficient reactor of its type in the world and as such offered a unique opportunity for exploring the peacetime application of atomic energy, and especially its use as an energy source for electric power. It was decided, therefore, that the program of research and development at Chalk River should be continued and expanded. In 1951 the decision was made to construct a second reactor which would have a dual purpose-production and research. This new reactor, called the NRU reactor, is of a similar type to the NRX reactor but much more advanced in design and of much higher power.
These decisions affecting the post-war program in atomic energy were reflected in the Atomic Energy Control Act of 1946. The intent and purpose of the act were set out in its preamble as follows:
It is essential in the national interest to make provision for the control and supervision of the development, application and use of atomic energy, and to enable Canada to participate effectively in measures of international control of atomic energy which may hereafter be agreed upon . . .
The act provided for the establishment of an atomic energy control board which would be responsible for the over-all direction of the program and for administering the various types of security regulation which were required in the program. However, it seemed unwise to disturb the existing arrangement whereby Eldorado had direct responsibility for the raw materials program.

Atomic Energy Control Act and the national research council had direct responsibility for the research and development program. There was no great difficulty in the case of Eldorado, since its board of directors had reported to a minister during the war years. This arrangement was continued in the post-war years. The president of Eldorado was appointed a member of the atomic energy control board, in order that the board might be fully informed as to developments in the raw materials field. In practice, therefore, the authority of the atomic energy control board in relation to the raw materials program has been confined largely to the administering of security regulations affecting the disclosure of information.
The position with respect to the Chalk River project was somewhat more complicated. It seemed desirable that the atomic energy control board should deal with questions of policy, but at the same time that operating responsibility should be retained by the national research council. The atomic energy control board entered into an agreement with the national research council whereby it delegated to the national research council responsibility for operating the Chalk River project subject to direction by the board in matters of policy including the approval of the operating and research budgets. The president of the national research council was appointed to the atomic energy control board in 1946, and became its president in 1948. This arrangement prevailed until April 1, 1952, when the Chalk River project was incorporated. The new company, Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, was incorporated under the powers of the atomic energy control board, and its board of directors reported to the atomic energy control board. The company was to have operating responsibility for the Chalk River project, but the atomic energy control board was to retain responsibility at the policy level and for the approval of operating and research budgets. The president of the atomic energy control board was appointed as president of the new company.
When these several and somewhat complicated administrative arrangements were made, it was recognized that changes might be necessary as the program developed. The administrative organization of the two phases of the program, which I have just described, was an attempt to provide adequate but flexible control during the period of transition from the wartime program with its shortterm objectives to the peacetime program with its long-term objectives.
We are now passing from this transitional or second stage of the program to a third stage. The present amendments to the Atomic Energy Control Act are intended to provide

for administrative machinery which will meet the demands of this third stage of the program.
Before I discuss the proposed amendments I should like to comment briefly on the significant developments in the program with particular reference to its long-term objectives.
The work at Chalk River has reached the point where we now believe that it should be possible to produce atomic power within a range of cost which will be economic. To be more specific, we now see the possibility of producing atomic power at a cost which will be comparable to the cost of power generated from a steam plant using coal at $8 per ton. This has important implications for both the raw materials and the research programs, implications which suggest that the time has come when the two programs should be more closely integrated.
I have mentioned previously that the two reactors at Chalk River were designed to use heavy water as the moderator and natural uranium as the fuel. The atomic power feasibility study which is now being carried out at Chalk River in co-operation with the Hydro Electric Power Commission of Ontario is aimed at the development of an outline specification for a power reactor which will also use natural uranium as the fuel. It will be obvious, therefore, that the availability of a continuing supply of uranium is an important factor in the feasibility study and the developments which must follow from that study. Fortunately, our efforts to increase the production of uranium have been successful. Eldorado has expanded its production at Port Radium and last June brought into production a new mine at Beaverlodge, Saskatchewan. At the present time the production of uranium is three times as great as it was at the end of the war. The prospector and the mining industry are also making a major contribution to the raw materials program. A discovery in the Beaverlodge area by a private company late in 1952 gives every promise of being a large producer. It is expected that this property will be in production late in 1955. Other discoveries have been made in the Blind River and Haliburton areas of Ontario, several of which will also be producers. We can now estimate that the production of uranium in 1956 will be roughly eight times as grea as it was at the close of the war. While, ai I have indicated, the immediate objective of the raw materials program is to produce uranium for military use, it is reasonable to expect that in striving for this objective we will obtain a knowledge of our uranium resources which would not otherwise be

available. The program, therefore, has a long-term as well as a short-term objective. Since it is not possible at this time to estimate the amount of uranium which will be needed for a large-scale civilian application of atomic energy we are fortunate in having a guaranteed market which will provide a stimulus to production pending the day when we will be able to establish the level of civilian demand.
The importance of atomic fuel as a source of power will depend on the cost of producing it translated into cost per kilowatt hour of electric energy generated. In one sense the problem might be said to be economic rather than technical, since it has now been demonstrated that it is possible to design and operate a reactor which produces heat. In fact the technical and economic factors are inseparable. All of the reactors now in existence were costly to build and are expensive to operate. Most of them were designed to produce plutonium for the military program. If there were to be a continuing market for plutonium it would be possible to treat the heat as a by-product and thus produce low-cost power. There are two objections to this approach. First, a reactor designed primarily for the production of plutonium would not have the most desirable characteristics as a producer of heat for the generation of power. Second, it would be unwise to assume that the military demand for plutonium will continue at the present level for an indefinite period. A cut-back in demand, or a cessation of demand, would throw the full cost of the reactor and its operation against the production of heat, with a resulting cost per kilowatt hour which would be prohibitive. Therefore, we must find a way of designing a reactor which can be made self-sustaining-economically speaking-as a producer of heat. This is the main objective of the research program at Chalk River. It is a job which requires great genius in fundamental research, and great skill in design and engineering. The organization of the Chalk River project reflects this twofold need. It consists of two divisions: a division of research and development, and a division of industrial operations. The first is engaged in fundamental and applied research in nuclear physics, chemistry and allied fields. The second operates the reactors and the other services associated with them. The activities of the two divisions are very closely related and highly interdependent.
Measured strictly in terms of dollars a research program of this breadth and magnitude must be costly. In assessing the need for the large expenditure required we must
Atomic Energy Control Act keep in mind the ultimate benefits, which it will bring to the Canadian economy.
Already we are beginning to reap some of those benefits. Radioisotopes produced in the NRX reactor for use in medical treatment and research, and industrial processes, are now available and their number and quantity will increase. The commercial products division of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited is responsible for marketing these isotopes and for developing new uses for them. This division will shortly move to a new building in Ottawa which is fully equipped with all the facilities needed for carrying out its program. It has been the policy to work closely with the medical profession and industry in the development of uses for radioisotopes. This policy will be continued and expanded.
The second benefit we hope to derive from the Chalk River project is atomic power. We can only assess the importance of this contribution in terms of the probable future power demand and the resources which will be available to meet that demand. If the current rate of annual increase in power demand, which is approximately 6 per cent, continues we shall require something like an installed capacity of 40,000,000 kilowatts by 1979, as compared with the present installed capacity of 10,000,000 kilowatts. Our total estimated hydro potential of 50,000,000 kilowatts, of which we are now using approximately 20 per cent, will certainly not all be available for use in existing industrial areas since many of the hydro sites are located in remote districts. It would appear that of the total estimated hydro potential of 50,000,000 kilowatts, some 30,000,000 kilowatts might be in use by 1979, leaving a deficiency of 10,000,000 kilowatts to be met from thermal sources. If conventional fuelburning plants were used to supply this deficiency these plants would have to provide generating capacity equivalent to 100 per cent of our present generating capacity. This would mean an eightfold increase in our present steam plant capacity.
Any assessment of the cost of existing thermal sources in terms of the Canadian power picture as a whole is complicated by the fact that in some regions coal or oil, or natural gas, or all three, are available in substantial quantities and at low costs; whereas in other regions there are no indigenous thermal fuels. In the latter areas thermal fuels must be imported or brought from great distances within Canada. It is in these areas that atomic power should fill the gap, and it so happens that certain of them have experienced the largest increase in power requirements, a condition which is likely to continue.

Atomic Energy Control Act
While the figures I have used in this rough forecast of power requirements may be subject to future correction, the conclusion is inescapable that as our economy expands we must expect a continuing rise in power consumption. The availability of power will be a condition of our growth in the future as it has been a condition of our growth in the past, and it is within this context that the expenditures on the development of atomic power must be considered.
It is evident that if atomic energy is to make a major contribution to our power resources we must be self-sufficient at each stage in the process. We do not now enjoy this self-sufficiency. Eldorado's final product is an uranium oxide; whereas the fuel needed for the Chalk River reactors is uranium metal. At the present time the conversion of oxide to metal is carried out in the United States. That this should be so is simply a matter of economics. The volume of raw material production in Canada until recently did not warrant the production of uranium metal. With the increased production to which I have referred we think it may be possible to produce uranium metal in Canada at a satisfactory cost. As a first step in this direction Eldorado is installing a new and improved process in the Port Hope refinery. With this process it will be possible to refine a product which can be entered to a metal processing circuit without further purification. The alterations to the plant and the equipment required will cost $2,500,000. The work will begin immediately. The research and development division of Eldorado is also studying the technique of uranium metal production.
The Canadian program of atomic power development has not had the same publicity as similar programs in the United Kingdom and the United States. It should not be assumed from this that we are lagging behind in this new and important field. The quality of our effort is recognized by our British and American associates as being equal to that in the United Kingdom and in the United States. Possibly we have been overly cautious in our publicity policy. This seemed the better course until such time as the results of the research and development program could be expressed in reasonable concrete terms. We believe that time has now come. As a first step towards providing more information on the program, a power symposium was held at Chalk River last September. Certain of the papers presented at the symposium have now been published. As a second step it has been decided to set up an advisory committee on atomic power consisting of the senior executive officers of all


the power commissions and power corporations in Canada. The purpose of this committee is to inform those responsible for producing power in Canada of the nature and scope of the program at Chalk River. We would also hope that the committee would assist in evaluating the possible economic importance of atomic power in the various regions of the country.
Under the provisions of the present Atomic Energy Control Act, the atomic energy control board has two main functions. First, it has the power, either directly or through other agencies reporting to it, to conduct research and production operations in connection with atomic energy. Second, the board has the power to make regulations. The proposed amendments to the act provide that the first of these responsibilities shall be transferred to the minister who is the chairman of the committee of the privy council on scientific and industrial research. The minister may cause activities in the research and production field to be carried out by a company or companies.
It is proposed that Eldorado Mining and Refining Limited will continue to have responsibility for production and procurement in the raw materials field, and that Atomic Energy of Canada Limited will continue to have responsibility for the operation of the Chalk River project. However, the name of the latter company will be changed to Nuclear Research Limited, a name more properly descriptive of the activities at Chalk River.
In order that the program in the two fields may be more closely integrated it is proposed to incorporate a holding company which will hold the stock of Eldorado Mining and Refining Limited, and Nuclear Research Limited. This company will be called Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. The company will be responsible for the over-all direction of the program including the approval of operating and capital budgets. It will report to a minister-the chairman of the committee of the privy council on scientific and industrial research-who will hold the stock in trust for Her Majesty.
By this means the raw materials and research programs will be under the general direction of a single agency as is now the case in the United States and in the United Kingdom.
The atomic energy control board will retain its present responsibility for establishing and administering regulations subject to the approval of the governor in council. The board will also continue to report to the minister who is the chairman of the committee of

the privy council on scientific and industrial research. I hope that the day is not too far distant when many of the regulations now in effect can be removed. The existing regulations affecting the disclosure of information on atomic energy are similar to those now in effect in the United States and in the United Kingdom. The declassification of information in the three countries is dealt with by a committee of which the three countries are the members. This committee has already recommended the declassification of much technical information. So long as the need for regulation exists, it is believed that the atomic energy control board as presently constituted is the best agency for dealing with the problem.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS CONSOLIDATING ACTIVITIES OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must admit that as time has gone by in recent months I have become more and more anxious about Canada's position, as related to the United States and the United Kingdom, in the field of atomic research and development. This anxiety grew, I suppose, from reading the numerous and considerable reports of various achievements in both the United States and the United Kingdom in this field. After reading recent debates in the British House of Commons on the same subject one could not help wondering if Canada was maintaining its position relative to these other countries in this very important and highly competitive field, and if we were holding the very high position we had established during the last war.
I am pleased now to have some of this anxiety relieved by the statement of the minister. I must admit I was not counting on the characteristic he has just demonstrated, that of having hidden his light under a bushel for quite some time. However, I think the time has now come when as much publicity as possible should be given to the potentialities and possibilities of this new and great discovery, the use of atomic power for industrial purposes.
In that connection I should like to quote briefly from a news report resulting from an interview with Dr. C. J. Mackenzie, chairman of the atomic energy control board, and former president of the national research council who, in an interview with the Southam news services, made the following interesting statement:
1.	The time has now been reached when there is real danger of the people of the western world slowing down atomic research by the enforcement of too-rigid security measures.
2.	From here on, the less secrecy and the more people involved, the faster Canada and the world at large will be able to derive peacetime benefits from the atom.
Atomic Energy Control Act
I think those are very wise observations, because if we shut ourselves up in an airtight chamber of security we may not realize the progress which is being made in other parts of the world, and we may fall into the error of tending to rest on our laurels or become complacent.
It is not my intention, even if it were in order, to attempt to review the whole field *-and a very important field it is-of the activities of Canada in this matter of atomic research. However, there is one point upon which I should like to base my remarks for the next few minutes. I refer of course to the use of atomic energy for industrial purposes. I am delighted that the minister has now stated that we in Canada have reached a third stage of development in the atomic field, and that already a power committee has been set up for one purpose, among others, of making known to the main organizations in this country concerned with producing cheap electric power for industrial and civilian purposes a knowledge of the progress which has been made in relation to the use of atomic energy for those purposes.
Apparently in the United States for quite some time these possibilities have been vividly recognized, and the possibilities of the use of atomic power for industrial purposes has been greatly advanced by the high priority research done there in connection with the atomic powering of submarines. Recently in the United States they have launched a submarine which will have the capacity of sailing completely around the world without refuelling. Although I have no definite knowledge on this point, I should imagine that the power plant in a submarine of that type could be easily converted for civilian uses, provided it is economically feasible to do so.
Recently I read a news report setting out the opinion of an American expert in the power field. While, admittedly, this is only an opinion, it would be interesting to see what he said. This was his view:
Power plants using atomic energy may be competing favourably in the next ten years with those burning oil, a widely known petroleum executive predicts.
I do not want to take up the time of the house by making extensive quotations to illustrate that point; but I think it would be of interest to bring to the attention of the house the progress being made in the United Kingdom in the field of atomic power as applied to industrial uses. Sir David Eccles, speaking in the House of Commons in the United Kingdom on March 1, had this to say:
We are looking ahead beyond the race to pile up atomic weapons. Of course, at the moment the

Atomic Energy Control Act production of weapons must remain the major task of the program, but such progress has been made on the civilian side, here and abroad-and no one wants Britain to fail behind-that no time should now be lost in preparing for the day when the civilian uses of atomic energy are as important to our economy as the weapons now are to our defence.
And he goes on to say further:
Now a change is taking place, and there is no need to develop the peaceful uses of fissile materials in the dark. Parliament and industry ought now to know what is going on.
I hope that that is an opinion which is shared by the minister, because I feel it is important that parliament and the country generally should be kept as well posted as possible in the possibilities of the uses of atomic energy for peaceful purposes in the years ahead. Because I believe if we are well posted it will prevent, on the one hand, a supposition that atomic power perhaps will make obsolete all other methods of producing power. On the other hand, it would ensure against the danger of the opportunities in the atomic field being passed by, by those who are concerned with the production of atomic power and in the use of atomic radioactive products in many fields of research and in other ways as well. Sir David Eccles went on to say further:
The government believe that there is plenty of room for international collaboration on the peaceful development of atomic energy. Here is the seed of great things to come. A generation from now, we may hope, there will be power stations all over the world operated by men trained in Britain.
In connection with international co-operation in this field, it is interesting to note that the United Kingdom is now a member of an organization which has been set up in Europe, called the European organization for nuclear research, the purpose of which is to co-operate in basic research into the question of atomic power.
I was glad to hear the minister say that there is close continuing co-operation between Canada, the United States and Great Britain in this field; but I would not like to think that the possibilities of even wider co-operation on an international scale might be forgotten. There is another quotation from the same speech in the British House of Commons which I found enlightening, in which Sir David Eccles recited briefly the development which had been made with regard to research into the application of atomic energy for the production of electric power. He said:
It looks as though the most important use will be for the generation of electricity, and the house may wish to know how we see the electricity program taking shape. At present, we are building the first atomic power station in this country at Calder Hall, in Cumberland. When this prototype


has demonstrated the soundness of the design, the electricity authorities-the B.E.A. and the Scottish electricity boards-will be free to place orders for other reactors of this or improved types.
I am glad the minister has indicated that something parallel to this is anticipated in this country and will be, I hope, carried on in the near future, because certain areas of this country, especially the maritime provinces, which have been economically depressed for some time, might be put in a position to compete more favourably with the more highly industrialized areas of this country if it were possible to supply them with cheap electric power. The key to that problem might eventually, in the relatively near future, be found in the use of atomic energy for the production of power, because in the cost of this fuel transportation is not a problem. It would be possible to locate generators in areas where other types of fuel are not readily available in the immediate vicinity. Sir David Eccles went on to say with regard to another program:
But I now have to tell the house that our people are ready to go ahead with the far more powerful and dramatic project. It has been decided to build a big, fast reactor, of the "breeder" type, to which the minister of supply referred in the house on 26th January and 16th November of last year. This plant will be constructed at Dounreay, in Caithness. An enterprise of this kind requires a very large site-at least some hundreds of acres-in open country, but it must be within reach of a labour supply and the amenities of community life. It must be on the coast, both for the discharge of the effluent and to provide sea water for cooling. It also requires a very large supply of fresh water.
Dounreay meets all these requirements better than any other site. It has the further advantage that development there should make a very big contribution to the revival of the highlands.
Therefore in the United Kingdom they are already anticipating the taking of steps to correct the very conditions that exist not only in the highlands of Scotland but in certain areas of this country. I refer to the maritime provinces, and it is particularly applicable to the province from which I come.
I refer of course to the importance of international co-operation in the field of atomic research and in the sharing of knowledge in this field. The minister may say-and perhaps rightly so-that is more a question for the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson); but nevertheless I think a great obligation rests with the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe) to see that every facility is made available on an international scale which will forward the interests of the peaceful use of atomic energy without endangering in any way our defence program in that connection.
I was interested to read in the debates of the British House of Commons a paragraph

of a speech made by Mr. Eden in a debate on foreign affairs in connection with this very problem. This is what he said:
So far as Her Majesty's government are concerned-and who can doubt that it is the position of the Canadian government, too?-we shall do everything-
I hope Mr. Eden is right in having no doubt that it is also the position of the Canadian government. I continue:
-we shall do everything that lies in our power by contribution, direct or indirect, to bring about the success of these discussions on atomic issues. I can tell the house that we felt-I know that I did and I think my right hon. friend did also-the impact of this topic so tremendous on the whole of our thought and discussion that some of the things we have discussed-foreign office problems of detail -important though they are, seemed puny pawns in comparison with the great danger that these master chessmen present to the future of the world. I wanted to say that to the right hon. gentleman because I think it is our biggest issue in international relations.
Mr. Eden was referring to the possibility of international co-operation in the field of atomic research. I cannot express how strongly I feel, Mr. Speaker, that man's discovery of the release of atomic energy is by far the greatest step in a scientific way that civilization has made in this century. It is opening up a new era, and I hope that the government has a lively awareness of the implication which atomic energy holds both from the point of view of destruction and from the point of view of progress which can be achieved from the wise and co-operative use of atomic power in industry and in other ways. These possibilities are magnificently expressed by Sir Winston Churchill, in a speech he made in the British House of Commons not so long ago. If the house will bear with me I would like to quote from his speech because he expresses his views on the situation much better than I could. He states:
There is no doubt that if the human race are to have their dearest wish and be free from the dread of mass destruction, they could have, as an alternative, what many of them might prefer, namely, the swiftest expansion of material well-being that has ever been within their reach, or even within their dream.
By material well-being I mean not only abundance but a degree of leisure for the masses such as has never before been possible in our mortal struggle for life. These majestic possibilities ought to gleam, and be made to gleam, before the eyes of the toilers in every land, and they ought to inspire the actions of all who bear responsibility for their guidance. We. and all nations, stand, at this hour in human history, before the portals of supreme catastrophe and of measureless reward. My faith is that in God's mercy we shall choose aright.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS CONSOLIDATING ACTIVITIES OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister this afternoon has introduced a bill which indicates that the government is proceeding toward what he termed
83276-342J
Atomic Energy Control Act the third stage of Canada's atomic development. This follows quite logically from the steps that the house, the country, and the government have taken in the years which have passed.
This is an amendment to the Atomic Energy Control Act which I think is in line with the conception that the house had when the minister introduced the Atomic Energy Control Act several years ago, in I believe 1946. I think probably one of the most interesting parts of the statement he made this afternoon, outside the mechanics of the bill itself expanding the power and looking for methods of co-ordination and control in the development of this great source of energy, was the fact that already at the Chalk River plant atomic power production is in sight, and that it is in sight in an economic way so that ere long we may have the production of atomic power produced electricity based in cost on the equivalent of coal at $8 per ton.
That, it seems to me, is a very interesting announcement, and marks a very important achievement for our plant at Chalk River. Having visited that plant on two or three occasions, and having met the people who are in charge of it I have been deeply impressed by the ability and by the energy of the scientific officers who are directing the work there, and also by the enthusiasm of those young scientists who are occupied in the actual development of the project itself.
I believe that had it not been for the fact that the world discovered atomic energy in the closing days of the war, or perhaps it is more accurate to say during the war, then greater progress might have been made in the industrial use of atomic power. Unfortunately, most nations who discovered or developed atomic energy have been engaged in a race to produce atomic weapons of war, while Canada has not been engaged directly in that race. Consequently, the efficiency of our reactors, and the fact that we have now proceeded along the way to the point where the economic production of atomic energy for electrical purposes is in sight, is, I think, something of which we may be proud, and for which we may feel grateful.
I share the view that what we are going to experience in the next few years is something in the way of a new and more profound industrial revolution. Those of us who know the history of our present industrial system know that when coking coal was discovered in the early part of the eighteenth century combined with the discovery of the power of steam a little later by Thomas Watt, the results brought about an industrial revolution, and then when we had electricity

Atomic Energy Control Act and the development of electric power from coal, and subsequently from hydroelectric power, we once again saw a great forward movement of industrial production and expansion.
I think we can all agree with the closing words by Sir Winston Churchill quoted by the hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean) to the effect that what mankind will see in the next generation will dwarf anything that mankind has seen in any similar generation in our history. That is, of course, if we are wise enough to maintain the peace of the world, and if we are wise enough to cooperate with other nations in exchanging scientific views and the results of research among the nations.
I think one of the limiting factors over the last few years has been the fact that there has not been this free exchange of scientific information. We have had only limited exchange between Britain, Canada and the United States owing to the fact that so much of the information was classified and on the secret list. Thus we have not been able to make the exchange of information that would perhaps have been beneficial to us all.
This possibility of an industrial revolution, not only in our own country and countries like ours, but all across the world is, I think, self-evident.
As was pointed out this afternoon, the transportation of fuel for atomic energy will not require the hundreds of railway cars such as are now required in the transportation of coal, because quite small quantities of fissionable material can be transported to the ends of the world. Not only will that perhaps help areas such as the maritime provinces in Canada, and I hope that will materialize, but it will assist in many of the backward areas of the world where there is no hydroelectric power, where there is perhaps no coal, or if there is coal it is not yet developed, or its development would be very costly in terms of money and labour. Also where there is no oil or natural gas atomic energy may solve the problem of producing power required for the industrialization of what we sometimes term the backward areas, or which might better be described as the undeveloped areas of the world.
This bill which is introduced today is one to which I think we should give our support. It does, of course, give the minister even wider powers than he has today, but in the development of atomic energy I think that is quite justified.
I also wish to say that I think the idea of now centralizing the various phases of


atomic power research and development is a wise one, and the setting up of a holding company to centralize this control is also wise. The bill gives the minister power to set up subsidiary organizations as they become necessary, and I am glad to note, and I think it is the only way that atomic energy development can be undertaken, that the original conception of carrying out at least the main features of atomic development are to be kept carefully under public control. That is the situation in Great Britain.
As we move along I am sure that we shall find it economic and useful to preserve the control within the orbit of government, responsible to this parliament or to the provincial legislatures. That does not mean to say that certain results of this control and of development should not be made available to industry. I am not arguing that way at all. What I am arguing is that atomic power, as such, is too important to be allowed to pass away from the complete control of the public authority. I have been here long enough to have heard even outstanding Conservatives as well as others express regret that in former days some of the great resources of the country were allowed to slip from the public domain.
This bill carries forward the original idea which the minister and the government presented to the house in 1946. I was impressed also by what the minister said about the possibility of the demand for electric energy in the next few years. I think he said that by 1979 we would require 40 million kilowatts. That is a tremendous increase in electric power. As he said, while we have in this country a potential of hydro power which is much greater than that, nevertheless much of that potential is so far removed from the centres of population that it may not be economically feasible or desirable to use that hydro power. Consequently, if we have this alternative source requiring less in the way of heavy equipment and certainly less in the way of mining coal and transporting coal from one part of the country to another, we have an asset that may be of inestimable benefit to this expanding country. I am saying now that I share the view of the minister-and I believe it is that of most members of the house-that this country is going to expand and is going to become greater than we have yet known it.
I sometimes look back over my nearly 45 years in the country, particularly in western Canada, and remember that some 30 years ago I shared the view of a good many people, on the prairies at least, who thought that we had passed through the pioneer stage of the country and were approaching, as it were, the zenith of our production. How wrong was

that opinion of 30 years ago! In the last 10 or 15 years we have been able to see that we are only on the verge of the great expansion this country will see, with its remarkable resources.
As the minister pointed out this afternoon we are extremely fortunate indeed to have discovered, in recent years, rich deposits of uranium. Apparently they are more widespread than we thought they were. In the northern parts of the prairie provinces, and particularly in my own province of Saskatchewan, valuable finds have been made and valuable developments are taking place in the production of this source of atomic power. But at Blind River and elsewhere in Ontario and probably, from some indications, in the maritime provinces other sources may be found.
Then of course we are not limited to uranium. We now know that there are other sources which may be available to us and which may be mined in this country in the future. While at the moment we know less about those sources than we know of uranium, nevertheless they may yet be sources of great power. This country is so highly mineralized and so richly endowed by Providence, or by nature, as you will, with these valuable minerals and resources that it seems to me that Canada has a great future based upon energy derived, in part at least, from atomic power. Consequently it is important that this house should support the minister and the government in legislation of this description which preserves to the people of Canada, through the parliamentary institution, the direction and control of what, it seems to me, is in the future to be the greatest source of power bringing about an industrial revolution which the mind of man yet perhaps can scarcely conceive.
My hon. friend spoke of the blessings that this development might bring to the peoples of the world-if we can maintain peace, if we can exchange information and so on-in terms of improved standards of living, in terms of increased production and in terms of leisure. After all, if we have the means for the right use of leisure and if we educate our people to the right use of leisure and provide them, of course, as I said a moment ago, with the means to enjoy that leisure-I refer to the cultural means-the world can look forward to something better and greater than it has ever known. I believe that atomic energy will be one of the vehicles to bring about a great industrial and social revolution. As we speak of the industrial revolution of 200 years ago, so shall future generations speak of the industrial revolution in the second half of the twentieth century. In
Atomic Energy Control Act the generations that come after us I believe the great source of power that we are now developing in Canada and that has been developed in other parts of the world-if, as I say, we can only come to international agreements on the use of these resources- will give to the world an opportunity for a better life than we can even faintly visualize at the present time.

think that opens up very interesting possibilities. Mr. Speaker, the Atomic Energy Control Act will give the atomic energy control board the power to conduct research and production operations with respect to atomic energy in Canada. It has become apparent that it would be desirable to place these operations under a board under the jurisdiction of one minister, with the board reporting to the minister. I am sure that we know that rapid strides have taken place in the last decade in connection with atomic energy. We were not aware until the statement of the minister today of the great potential that exists for Canadians. Much credit for this great development must go to Canada's able scientists under the dynamic leadership of the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe). However, I feel that the words "atomic energy" will, whenever used, conjure up in the minds of most Canadians a picture of horror, total destruction and the very annihilation of life itself.
We have heard of the lethal qualities of atomic energy, of the destructive capacity of the A-bomb and the even greater volume and gigantic destructive capacity of the H-bomb. I think members of the house and people generally have expressed concern with regard to this destructive quality. In the house on April 14 last hon. members expressed their opinions on this subject and questioned the

Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson). On that occasion he stated, as found at page 4073 of Hansard:
The United Nations general assembly, by resolution of November 28 last year, suggested that the disarmament commission-
On which Canada is represented.
-would seek by agreement to work out arrangements for the elimination of all major weapons adaptable to mass destruction, and for effective international control of atomic energy to ensure the prohibition of atomic weapons and the use of atomic energy for peaceful purposes only.
Subsequently, on April 29, 1954, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), acting as Secretary of State for External Affairs, reported to the house that a subcommittee of the United Nations on disarmament had been formed and that Canada's Secretary of State for External Affairs would be Canada's representative on that commission. This should result in substantial progress being made in the finding of a solution to the problem of the destructive features of atomic energy. All members of this House of Commons, and citizens of Canada, will utter a prayer and express a fervent hope that atomic energy may never be used anywhere in the world for these purposes. I fear that we have placed far too great an emphasis on the wartime efficiency of this great discovery, and we have not looked to the peacetime uses of atomic energy which could bring great advantages and benefits to our people.
Today we welcome the words of the Minister of Defence Production, who has dealt practically entirely in his remarks with what might be done in the way of peacetime advantages of this great force. If the use of atomic energy could be directed along proper channels, much happiness and consolement may come to suffering humans. I gather that great efficiency can be made available to the great industrial machines of this country and the other countries of the world.
As I am not a scientist I shall not attempt to explain the chemical reaction that goes on to produce the breaking up of nuclear fission. I shall content myself with bringing to the mind of the members, Mr. Speaker, the one principal objective of the peacetime use of atomic energy, namely the production and use of radioisotopes which have been referred to by the minister this afternoon for medical, industrial and research purposes. While the use of isotopes is international, it seems best to me to discuss particularly the Canadian program. We are all proud in Canada of the atomic reactor that has been developed at Chalk River, and also of the diligence which has been applied to the production and distribution of isotopes which come from it.
Atomic Energy Control Act
What is a radioisotope? It has been defined as an ordinary element which has had its atomic masses increased by the capture of the neutron.	Its chemical and physical
properties remain the same except it decays giving off radiation.
What are the practical applications of radioisotopes? In the field of chemistry, atomic energy has a wide use in tracer studies and the separation and discovery of various elements in chemical analysis. The isotope can be used in industrial development to study foundation movements and the porosity of soil. The amount of moisture in soil can be definitely ascertained by making assays to determine the content. With regard to soil movements and disturbing equilibrium conditions, economic savings are probably to be found in preventive measures. A good knowledge of soil moisture content can simplify construction and reduce maintenance costs.
Static electricity causes time loss and fire hazard in a number of industrial operations. The use of radioactive static eliminators, developed and sold by Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, has become widespread. In the case of the ordinary printing press, these static eliminators, I am told, by providing machine-jogging for presses rather than hand-jogging will save in one day $200 or $300 a bar, the cost of the static eliminator. The cost of the bar, therefore, would be saved in the first day's operation. It is desirable to eliminate static from rotogravure operations in printing, as there is a great fire hazard because sparks from static electricity may commence a fire in the inflammable ink. Today the newspapers of Canada are now employing these bars which are also sold by Atomic Energy of Canada Limited.
Another example of the use of the portable neutron is the logging of petroleum bore-holds. I am informed that they have been found very useful in western Canada. There is, of course, the possibility of atomic energy being used in the development of electricity, and that has been dealt with fully today by the minister. It seemed fantastic that within a period of three to five years we should be able to provide for industry in this country great sources of electric energy that are urgently needed. It was reported in the newspapers the other day that the chairman of the Ontario Hydro Electric Power Commission had stated that they would be able to develop power within the course of five years. From the lips of the minister today, it would seem that this is not beyond the realm of possibility.

Atomic Energy Control Act
I come now to what seems to me to have been the greatest development in atomic energy, the discovery of a form of treatment for mankind. A notable milestone in Canada's cancer program was the development by Canadian government scientists of the cobalt 60 beam therapy unit. This apparatus, which provides a new and potent weapon to combat cancer, has received world-wide recognition and places Canada among the leaders in the light against cancer. The demand for these units, both here and abroad, is greater than can be met by the crown company, Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, which is still the world's only producer of this equipment.
It is just about three years ago since the first cancer patient underwent treatment of this kind in London's Victoria hospital. While the government scientists have been working on the development of cobalt 60 apparatus, similar equipment was developed by Dr. A. E. Johns independently in Saskatoon. Shortly after, government-built units were installed in Montreal, Toronto, Vancouver and Winnipeg. Only about a month or five weeks ago a new unit was installed in the city of Hamilton. The installation of Hamilton's unit brought to six the total number of units now in use in Canada. Canadian-built equipment has been provided for hospitals in the United States at New York, Chicago and Minneapolis. Atomic Energy of Canada Limited has provided units for hospitals in London, England, and for a medical centre in Italy. Plans are now being worked out, in co-operation with provincial authorities and professional men in the cancer field, for the development of a program which will provide these units across the country. I might say that the Department of National Health and Welfare has had a great part in the distribution of these units to the various medical centres throughout Canada. It is the hope of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited that cobalt 60 units may be provided in every province, and particularly in those centres which have university students and university laboratories. The university centres may expect great progress in this field.
At the present time, as we have been told by the minister, Atomic Energy of Canada Limited is building a new and more powerful reactor which will increase the supply of cobalt available for the purpose, and it is expected that by December of this year it will be possible to step up the production of therapy units to two each month.
In my own province of Ontario there are already three units in operation. I understand that two additional ones are to be


built in the new Ontario cancer institute in Toronto. It is hoped that additional units will be provided in Windsor, Ottawa, Kingston and Port Arthur.
Only a short time ago I read in the newspapers that Mr. J. W. McConnell, an outstanding and philanthropic citizen of Montreal, had contributed one of these therapy units to the Royal Victoria hospital in that city at a cost of $80,000. I am sure that for those who are interested in the welfare of mankind, and who have the means to do it, may well contribute to this most worth-while charity. I commend Mr. McConnell for his most humanitarian act.
Great care must be exercised in the transportation of the cobalt bomb. The bomb consists of a small box about an inch and a half square filled with small pellets of cobalt that have been rendered radioactive by a year's cooking in the atomic reactor at Chalk River. It is encased in a huge lead box, about four feet long and two feet in diameter, in order that no danger will come to those who come in contact with this substance.
The treatment room is square and roomy. The operator works from a room adjacent, and is enabled to see what is going on by looking through a glass. The bomb sits in the centre of the room and the technician operates the machine from a radio-like box. Cobalt 60 radiations do not offer a positive cure for all forms of cancer. However, it* rays do provide a means of treating certain cancerous conditions more effectively than with either radium or X-ray. Moreover the new cobalt 60 units provide cancer treatments at a much lesser cost than was previously possible.
One cobalt 60 beam therapy unit costs in the neighbourhood of $60,000 to $80,000. It produces more radiation, I am advised, than medically-used radium worth millions of dollars. In contrast to the X-ray, the cobalt unit can do the work of a two-million-volt X-ray machine, which would cost about four times as much to build.
The development of the cobalt 60 beam therapy unit has brought treatment within the reach of millions of people in our community to whom otherwise this treatment would be denied. The development of this unit by the Canadian government is an achievement not only by the administrators of the plan, and the scientists of Canada, but also by the people of this country.
Today it has been my purpose to bring to the attention of hon. members, and to Canadians generally, the peacetime uses of this great force. I suppose that in a humble way we are doing something in the house today to encourage further development, and to

see that it is kept within the control of responsible authorities, in order that, in the future, people may have the benefit of these discoveries. It is in this spirit that we are endeavouring to expand and to promote the activities of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, under the direction of one of Canada's outstanding ministers, the Minister of Defence Production.

Before the bill receives second reading there are one or two words I wish to say about it. I was concerned when I heard the minister say that power could be produced from atomic sources which would equal the power produced from coal at about $8 a ton. I would not for a moment suggest that we should curtail the progress made in atomic energy, and particularly as it will apply to our industrial output. I think it is a sign of progress, just as much a sign of progress as is the development of our coal and gas; but it does raise a problem which is exceedingly important to this country, namely, what is going to happen to our coal mines? We have a great deal of trouble now in maintaining even a semblance of a coal industry. I read in the papers yesterday that the coal mines in Alberta are going to be reduced again this year by over 1,000 miners.
Two years ago they were reduced to the extent of about 2,000 miners. That is a considerable decrease in the number of miners who are employed in the coal mining industry. If we have the St. Lawrence project developed as expected we are going to produce another abundance of electric power for central Ontario which means that that too will enter into competition with coal from western Canada and eastern Canada as well. We have this new atomic energy program which is going to compete directly with coal as an energy producing product, and, indeed, the minister has even gone so far as to say that those in charge of these new atomic sources calculate that it will compete with the energy produced from coal at $8 a ton.
We out in western Canada certainly cannot place coal down here at $8 per ton, nor can they do so from Nova Scotia, or the provinces of Quebec or Ontario at that price. I am not suggesting to the government at this time what method they should adopt to keep the coal industry alive in view of the fact that we have this new form of energy entering into competition with the products of that industry, but it seems to me the government is going to have to assume the responsibility in some way or other for continuing to maintain our coal industry, at least at that level where we can call upon it in the event of an emergency.

The coal industry is rapidly dying out and if we were to call upon it immediately I am sure it could not even begin to meet the demand. In view of the development of atomic fuel it may be necessary to take some very drastic action in the form of subsidizing the coal industry, or we may have to curtail some of the imports of coal from the United States. It may well be that we will have to devise some method involving both these prospects. But it does seem to me, in view of the statement made by the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe) in regard to the production of power from atomic energy, that something must be done to maintain the coal industry in both western and eastern Canada. Atomic Energy Control Act he is the most outrageously optimistic member of the cabinet. Yet the figures of production of electricity he gave us, although startling, are pessimistic. He said that the current installed capacity of electric power is about ten million kilowatts, and 25 years from now it was estimated that it would be about 40 million kilowatts. Fantastic as that figure is I suggest it is quite conceivable that it could be much more. The right hon. gentleman said the rate of increase in consumption of power is about six per cent per annum. I think that rate of increase will increase still further as the years go by and within 25 years we are going to find ourselves, not only in Canada but in other countries, crying out loudly for power.
I am sure the minister knows as well as I do about the researches carried out into the matter of available materials for the creation of energy which exists in the world just now. An American has created a unit known as "Q". This emit is the equivalent of one billion billion British thermal units.
The figures are so vast that I can hardly conceive them, but he has made certain inquiries into the situation and his belief at the moment is that our present world consumption of energy is at the rate of some 20 Q's per century. By the time we come to the year 2,000 he estimates that consumption will be 100 Q's per century, or 100 billion billion b.t.u.'s.
Again, according to this gentleman, the known reserves of fossil energy-that is coal, oil, gas and so on-amount to about 80 Q's. Within a predictable number of years- within 75 years perhaps-we shall have used up all the known fossil reserves of energy in the world. It is therefore highly essential that we start now and examine much more carefully into the possible uses we can make of nuclear energy.
The minister said that it is expensive. I do not for a moment deny that it is. But I do not think we have been spending enough money on this aspect of governmental operations. For instance, two or three years ago there was an accident with regard to the NRX reactor and I believe- and here I am subject to correction-that the expense involved in bringing the NRX reactor back into working trim was taken out of the current budget. If that was so, did it not have an adverse effect upon the research which should have been carried on during these months and years? I think more money ought to be spent in this sort of basic research because it is vitally necessary.
I do not believe that nuclear power is going to be the last word in energy either,


because surely it is merely a transition from fossil energy to solar energy of some type or other. Very shortly our whole attention will have to be concentrated upon solar energy because there is only a known quantity of uranium in the world which can be built up, unless we manage to succeed in creating breeder plants, something which has been done in some measure in the United States but which has not yet been done in Canada, apparently, according to what the minister said. I would imagine the next step is to concentrate our efforts on creating a breeder plant. When we do that we shall then be in a position where we can approach those provinces which are especially in need of power and, with the help of the federal government and through public ownership in the provinces concerned, build breeder plants in those provinces in order to give them the power which they need.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: AMENDMENTS CONSOLIDATING ACTIVITIES OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intervene in this discussion merely to deal with one question which has been raised by my friend the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green), namely what provision has been made for and what is being discussed in relation to international control of atomic energy.
As the house knows,-indeed it was referred to this afternoon-a proposal was made by President Eisenhower last December by which there would be international co-operation through the United Nations in the peaceful use of and the peaceful progress that might be achieved through atomic energy. That proposal, which visualized a central international agency to which the contributing countries would make available raw material, which might itself construct a reactor for scientific purposes or which might help other countries to build reactors, has been initially discussed between the United States and the U.S.S.R. on a bilateral basis. The other countries chiefly concerned, including Canada, have been informed of the results of those discussions.
At the Geneva conference there was a meeting between the secretary of state of the United States and the foreign minister of the U.S.S.R. at which the reply of the U.S.S.R. was given to the approach made by the United States on this subject. That reply was discouraging in so far as the participation of the Soviet union in this international endeavour was concerned. The question now for consideration is whether those countries who wish to participate in such an international enterprise should go ahead without the U.S.S.R.

This project, however, has nothing to do with the international control of atomic energy for destructive purposes. As my hon. friend knows and as the house knows, that subject has been under discussion for a good many years, beginning back in 1946 when the United States, which then had sole possession of the atomic bomb, made certain proposals which would have brought the use of atomic energy for destructive purposes under international control. Those proposals and others have been discussed from time to time at the United Nations but, as the house knows, no agreement has been possible in respect of them.
As I mentioned in the house last week, at the present time a subcommittee of the disarmament committee of the United Nations is pursuing these discussions in London in private and in restricted session, in the hope that in that way

in view of the developments that have occurred since we first began to consult on this problem; tragic developments indeed if they are used for wrong purposes-this might make possible the kind of progress that we had not yet achieved. As I indicated last week, these discussions are still going on.
I noticed in the press the other day one optimistic statement as to the progress that has been made in London. From my contact with these discussions-and I attended some of the meetings-and from the reports which I have since received, I have not been able to arrive at any such optimistic conclusion. The difficulties have been clarified, but up to the present time at least the gap between the two positions with respect to the international control of atomic energy has not been closed.
All I can say is that while one cannot, I think, be too optimistic, the talks are still going on. If these talks were successful and if an international agreement for the control of atomic energy could be concluded-and we must all hope that it can one day be concluded-any agreement that we have been considering up to the present would not, I think-unless it included provision for international ownership of materials and processes -interfere with national development in this field for constructive purposes. It would merely deal with the use of atomic energy for destructive purposes. But even if you did not have international ownership, such control would require some form of international inspection and control inside national territory in order to make sure that atomic energy was being used for constructive purposes only and that the provisions of the agreement were being carried out. But that kind of inspection and control, and if international
Atomic Energy Control Act ownership were not included in any agreement which we might make, should not interfere with national progress in this field.

Hov/e (Minister of Trade and Commerce): Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank those who have taken part in this debate for their constructive approach to the subject that we have been discussing. It is a subject in which we all take great interest and is one that it is hard to break down into language that is familiar to those who have not been in close contact with the work on atomic energy.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) has raised a few points that I shall try to cover. In the first place I may say that there is no doubt that the amendments we are proposing to the Atomic Energy Control Act diminish the powers and authority of the control board. That is an evolution that I think is logical. Back in 1946 when we passed the act now under discussion control loomed large. We were quite conscious of the fact that plutonium is the substance used for peaceful applications of atomic energy, but it is also the substance used for the manufacture of A-bombs.
At that time knowledge of the production of plutonium was believed to be held in the United States, the United Kingdom and Canada, so that control of information, and particularly control of the raw materials from which plutonium is made, seemed very important. At that time it seemed wise to put the experimental work on atomic energy and the production of plutonium at Chalk River under the atomic energy control board. Therefore when we incorporated the operation at Chalk River we placed the stock of the corporation with the atomic energy control board.
The present situation seems to require a different form of organization, a form of organization where all the atomic energy operations, apart from the control functions, are concentrated in a single corporate body. We are still retaining the control functions, and only the control functions, in the atomic energy control board, and it is my thought that in a year or two or three those control functions may no longer be necessary. The basic information about atomic energy is widely disseminated now. Controls that were important three or four years ago are not so important today. However, there are certain controls over the distribution of raw materials and over certain information associated with the production of atomic energy which have not been declassified as yet. Therefore the

Atomic Energy Control Act control functions remain with the control board but the other operations are being assigned to a corporation which will be known as Atomic Energy of Canada Limited.
Under Atomic Energy of Canada Limited there will be two divisions, one the raw materials division, Eldorado Mining and Refining Limited. Its functions will not be changed, and the only change in the functions of the productive and experimental side will be that the name will be changed to-

speechtext:
-Nuclear Research Limited. In the proposed form of organization we are following exactly the pattern of organization in the United States. In the United States all functions associated with atomic energy are centred in the atomic energy commission which is appointed by the President and reports directly to the President. In the United Kingdom there has been a change in the same direction. Recently a corporation has been formed-I am not sure of the name-which will assume full responsibility for experimental and productive functions in the field of atomic energy and will report to a member of the government. I think it will be the president of the privy council of the United Kingdom.
Therefore we are adopting a form which has been found satisfactory to both the United States and Britain, and I think it will be a more workable form than the one we have used over the past seven or eight years. My hon. friend asked whether any United States cabinet minister has powers as extensive as those contemplated under this bill. The exact situation is that the functions have been and are being carried out by the President of the United States without the intervention of a cabinet minister. It is difficult to compare the situation in the United States with the situation in Canada due to the completely different forms of government. In the United States the legislative functions are completely separate from the executive functions. While the President has direct control of the field of atomic energy, he depends on congress to pass the legislation required in that field, and the legislators in their wisdom have established a commission on atomic energy which used to be headed by Senator McMahon. I am not sure who is the chairman now. I think it is Senator Hickenlooper.
That committee reviews the work on atomic energy from time to time and amends the existing legislation as it may decide after receiving the recommendations of the President. I think my hon. friend will know that I have never resisted any desire of the House of Commons to have a committee


on atomic energy. My hon. friend and I discussed earlier this session whether we should have a committee this year. I pointed out that the principal reactor at Chalk River was under repair-I am happy to say it is now back in operation-and I suggested that perhaps we might defer the committee until the next session of parliament. If a number of members indicate sufficient interest in the subject to warrant a committee on atomic energy or on research in general, as the committee may decide, at the next session, I would be very happy to agree. I think the committees have been useful in the past, and I think next year will be a very interesting one and one that will warrant the committee's study.
Then the hon. member asked why there are not more producing mines. Mining is a field that requires time for development. The only reason I know that there are not more producing mines is that development has not proceeded in any mine, except Rix-Athabasca, to the point where commercial deliveries can be made.
