speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house will be interested in a brief explanatory statement of the background and purposes of this bill. I shall make reference to the circumstances which led to the government's decision to

Diplomatic Immunities
propose the measure and say something about the legal necessity for enacting such legislation?
It has become apparent in recent years, as a result of constitutional developments within the commonwealth, that an anomaly existed in respect of the status of the diplomatic representatives exchanged between the various countries of the commonwealth. Before 1948 commonwealth high commissioners were generally considered to rank below foreign ambassadors in the diplomatic lists maintained by commonwealth governments. There was some doubt whether high commissioners were entitled to diplomatic privileges. High commissioners, as representatives of the different governments in the commonwealth, were not in reality representatives of foreign sovereigns and consequently, in law if not in practice, were not entitled to the customary immunities which the law accords to the diplomatic agents of foreign states. The commonwealth countries were thus placed in the curious position of affording, at least in law, greater rights to the representatives of foreign countries than to those of commonwealth countries. It seemed, therefore, that as a result of the association in the commonwealth the representatives of commonwealth countries must suffer disadvantages which, however intangible, are not compatible with the close ties of friendship between the governments of the commonwealth.
Since 1948, when at the commonwealth prime ministers' conference it was agreed that the status of high commissioners should be made to conform to that of foreign ambassadors, the various governments have been taking steps in that direction. Diplomatic privileges, such as tax and cusoms exemptions, had before 1948 been accorded to commonwealth representatives. The high commissioner has since then come to be recognized as equal in rank to the ambassador in matters of protocol. High commissioners have been permitted when eligible to assume the position of dean of the diplomatic corps in the various commonwealth countries. By an exchange of telegrams late in 1949 between the various prime ministers concerned it was agreed in principle that legislation should be enacted in each of the commonwealth countries to accord, on a reciprocal basis, diplomatic immunity to commonwealth representatives, thus placing them in the same position under the law in respect of immunities as the diplomatic representatives of foreign states. Such legislation has already been enacted in most of the countries of the commonwealth with the exception of Ceylon and Pakistan where similar legislation is being considered. Because of the
reciprocal feature in such legislation and because of the desirability of its aims, the government considers it appropriate to enact a corresponding law in Canada.
I should like to emphasize that this legislation is in no way concerned with the customary diplomatic privileges, such as tax and customs exemptions, which are already enjoyed by ambassadors and high commissioners, alike. It relates solely to immunity from legal process in Canada. It is intended to protect the valid interests of commonwealth governments and to permit their representatives to carry out their proper functions as members of diplomatic and consular missions in Canada.
However, it is important to remember that immunity is not accorded for the benefit of the individual in question, but of the state in whose service he is in order that he may fulfil his official duties with the necessary independence. A person entitled to diplomatic immunity is only immune from legal process and is still expected to comply with the law of the land, criminal and civil. As a matter of practice the conduct of the members of diplomatic missions should be exemplary and the immunity should exist only to preserve the independent function of the missions and to protect them from frivolous proceedings.
The bill before the house provides that commonwealth high commissioners, their official and domestic staffs and their families, and the families of their official staffs, shall be entitled to like immunity from suit and legal process as is accorded to foreign ambassadors, their official suite and family. The bill stipulates, however, that a member of the official or domestic staff who is a citizen of Canada is excluded from immunity except in respect of things done or omitted to be done in the course of the performance of his official duties, and the members of his family are entirely excluded. The bill also provides for the like inviolability of the residence, official permises and official archives of the high commissioner as is enjoyed by foreign ambassadors in this country.
The bill also contemplates the extension of consular immunity to commonwealth officials in Canada who perform duties substantially corresponding to those of foreign consuls. Consular immunity implies immunity from criminal and civil process but only with regard to the performance of official duties; it includes inviolability of official archives. Since it was not possible to foresee all the categories of commonwealth representatives which might be involved in this extension of consular immunity, it was considered preferable to make provision for such extension by proclamation. It is envisaged that such
[Mr. Pinard.l

immunity will be extended to commonwealth officials serving in Canada but outside Ottawa, as, for instance, trade commissioners, in which circumstances they might not be considered members of the official staff of their high commissioner in Canada.
No effort has been made in the bill, which is similar to the legislation already in force in Australia, New Zealand and the United Kingdom, to define the diplomatic and consular immunities. All that is said is that the commonwealth representatives are entitled to the like immunities as are accorded to a foreign envoy, or to the members of his official and domestic staff and the families concerned. It would be for the Canadian courts to decide in each case what these "like immunities" should be. The court would probably decide these matters by referring to the customary rules of international law as applied in Canada.
The bill makes provision for reciprocity as between Canada and the other countries of the commonwealth. The Canadian high commissioners and their staffs in most of the commonwealth countries are already accorded the immunities provided for in this bill. Legislation in these countries calls for reciprocal treatment. The remaining commonwealth countries contemplate legislation along similar lines. It is therefore considered desirable, in view of the principle of reciprocity, that parliament should take action now to ensure that commonwealth high commissioners in this country shall be accorded the same treatment which Canadian representatives receive in other commonwealth countries. It is the hope of the minister that the provisions of this bill will commend themselves to all hon. members, for he considers that this measure is noncontroversial and this necessary step in the orderly development of relations between members of the commonwealth can be taken with the full and warm approval of all parties.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EXTENSION TO COMMONWEALTH REPRESENTATIVES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat has reviewed in some degree the situation with regard to the diplomatic and consular immunities that have prevailed for generations as between foreign countries with their representatives in other countries. It is of interest to note he has stated that in 1948 the prime ministers of the various commonwealth countries agreed upon the necessity for this legislation. Similar legislation has been introduced in certain other commonwealth countries. If it were otherwise one might conclude that this was a step in a policy of attrition to remove and
Diplomatic Immunities
diminish commonwealth bonds. However, the agreement among the prime ministers that this legislation or something similar is necessary indicates another step in the gradual and unplanned development of the commonwealth and empire which began with Lord Durham's report and had its culmination in the Statute of Westminster.
It removes a rather anomalous situation, namely that the representatives of the commonwealth did not enjoy this immunity while representatives to other parts of the commonwealth such as would be enjoyed by representatives of foreign countries. It has its statutory background, in so far as foreign countries are concerned, in a statute passed in the reign of Queen Anne when the Russian ambassador at that time was arrested for owing some civil debt and was imprisoned. The result was that ill-feeling sprang up between England and Russia and legislation was passed in order to prevent a situation such as that again arising.
Since the beginning of the first war, and it is interesting to watch this trend, there has been a change in commonwealth relations, gradual, certain, and in some cases profound. Many have felt that these changes would weaken the commonwealth. But in point of fact while the commonwealth has no charter, constitution, or constitutional machinery, these steps which apparently constitute in themselves a weakening of the relationship actually have made for a strengthening in the purpose and unity of the commonwealth.
I agree with the hon. gentleman that this legislation is non-controversial. It is simply the implementation of an agreement among the prime ministers to remove what, on the face of it, was a paradoxical situation for commonwealth representatives. It places commonwealth representatives in an analogous position in so far as freedom from civil or criminal process is concerned as that now applicable to representatives from foreign countries.
While there are a few questions that will be asked when the bill goes into committee, generally speaking I think there will be agreement that this legislation is but one step forward in unifying the commonwealth and in actually bringing together in closer relationship the various parts of the commonwealth while maintaining their freedom under the Statute of Westminster.

We are indeed pleased to give our support to this bill. It is a very simple one, but it is significant; it suggests the march of history, and it gives us the opportunity to express once again our pride in the independence and autonomy of our nation, and also our pride in being a member of the commonwealth of nations, with its many peoples in all parts of the world.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EXTENSION TO COMMONWEALTH REPRESENTATIVES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say just a word or two in respect of this measure. When I first read of it and when it was brought down I noticed the title of the bill and I was rather pleased with it. We in this group have always desired to aid any measure whatsoever which would assist in bringing closer the ties of all the countries of the British commonwealth, and I think the bill does just that.
Now, I must say this, however, and simply to clear my own conscience, although this bill is not on a par altogether with previous measures which have been taken with respect to diplomatic immunity for those travelling to and from Canada. I recall that a few years ago the subject of diplomatic immunity came up with regard to members of the United


Nations. We did not oppose that measure or that principle, but I must confess that my conscience was not altogether clear with respect to that matter. As I have said before, I know this measure is not on a par with previous actions taken in regard to diplomatic immunity.
I cannot help feeling a deep responsibility, even though I am only a member of parliament, when we discover that there is growing up in our relationship with other nations, diplomatic representation by embassies and so forth which in reality have become, in some respects, nothing but hotbeds of spies. That is the truth.
I am not saying that such a thing is happening with respect to our own commonwealth countries. We are happy indeed that there is this gentlemanly and brotherly type of relationship between all nations of the commonwealth. These are brotherly ties. Even though some of these nations have been granted their independence in the last few years, nevertheless there is a strange and significant loyalty among all the countries of the commonwealth.
I must once again emphasize the fact that I believe that we can sometimes lean over backwards and go too far in this matter of diplomatic immunity. I know that what I am about to say does not come within the direct purview of this bill, but nevertheless I simply use it as an illustration. Not so long age we read of the happenings in Australia -which were similar to happenings which took place in Canada a few years ago- where one man of the Russian embassy, a high-ranking official, bolted and revealed tremendous truths concerning the operation of that spy ring within Australia, one of our commonwealth countries. You cannot read the first report of that commission which was set up in Australia to study the matter without having your hair almost stand on end when discovering the intrigue and what was happening in diplomatic circles in that country. When we offer these countries all the privileges that diplomats and embassies have, it is indeed shocking to discover that they are being used as centres from which radiate various intricate, clever and powerful rings of spies.
In that first report that was given on the recent Australian revelation it was stated that such things as code messages from Moscow had come in undeveloped films delivered to the embassy in Canberra in the diplomatic pouch. Here is what is meant by diplomatic immunity in the broad sense. These films had come in the diplomatic pouch which was not subject to search. These were films which any agent or official, if he wished, could destroy in an instant by exposing them

to the light. That is only one little incident that we glean from that one report. This whole thing emanated from the Russian embassy in Australia.
That sort of thing makes one rather wary concerning going too far in respect of this matter of diplomatic immunity. My own personal view is that when anything of that kind happens, action should be taken such as that which the Australian government took and that diplomatic relations should be broken off with any country that will abuse those privileges. As I said before, I know that that is not going to apply to our commonwealth countries. Nevertheless I use that as an illustration of a vital principle that is involved in matters of diplomatic immunity. Let us be most careful not to lean overboard or to go wild in respect of this matter of diplomatic immunity. As far as this bill is concerned, we are in favour of the measure.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. E. Harris (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL THE DECLARATION OF INTENTION
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 445, to amend the Canadian Citizenship Act.
He said: This bill requires only a very brief explanation, Mr. Speaker. The purpose of it is to do away with the present practice of asking an applicant for citizenship to file a declaration of intention at least one year prior to his application for citizenship. The

Canadian Citizenship Act declaration of intention has been a part of the citizenship procedure since the act was passed in the house in 1946. As a matter of fact, it dates back to a period during the war when, for certain purposes, a declaration was used for the first time.
In our experience it no longer contributes to the procedure in any way and only impedes it, as a matter of fact, to the extent that some candidate for citizenship, having waited five years and having fulfilled the residence requirements, suddenly discovers he has omitted to file a declaration of intention and then must wait a further year before his application can be processed. There is a further matter of cost, Mr. Speaker, in connection with the filing of this declaration by the applicant; it costs the department some money to print these forms, and it costs a staff to maintain them. We have examined the need for the declaration over the past twelve months, and have come to the conclusion it serves no useful purpose. All the inquiries we feel should be made can be made without it.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL THE DECLARATION OF INTENTION
speechtext:
The minister's explanation which elaborates somewhat on the explanatory note accompanying the bill seems to provide an adequate justification for the legislative proposal now before us. I cannot really believe that there would be any objection to the proposal to eliminate the necessity of filing a declaration of intention, although I believe we should ask the minister, when we come to the stage when questions may be asked, just what provision the government intends to make for ensuring that the information which might be elicited at the time of filing of the declaration will be adequately elicited later, and to ensure that sufficient precautions will be taken to establish that the applicant is indeed a qualified and suitable applicant. However those are matters of detail and as I say there seems to be no real reason why this proposal should not be adopted.
At this stage I want to point out something which I imagine has occurred to the minister, and that is that the indirect effect of abolishing this requirement of filing a declaration of intention is to remove the only surviving privilege now in existence with respect to those who are British subjects and wish to become Canadian citizens, that is subjects of Her Majesty from other parts of the commonwealth who come to Canada and wish to become Canadian citizens.
Under the present arrangement, everyone who comes to Canada and is a lawfully landed immigrant and wishes to become a Canadian citizen has to wait five years; and this includes British subjects from other

parts of the commonwealth. But a British subject does not have to file a declaration of intention. That is the only differentiation made between a British subject who wishes to become a Canadian citizen, and a nonBritish subject.
When the Canadian Citizenship Act was passed in 1946 we in the official opposition pointed out that in our opinion it did not give due recognition to the one effective approach that exists in the world today to a common or international citizenship brotherhood-the concept of being a subject of Her Majesty in whatever part of the commonwealth one might live. We urged then that persons coming from other parts of the commonwealth should not be specially privileged Canadian citizens, once they had become citizens. And I wish to make that clear, now, that at no time did we urge that we wanted any differentiation between citizens, no matter what their prior citizenship may have been. There should be no difference between Canadian citizens.
But we do think it proper to urge that recognition be given to those coming here from other parts of the commonwealth that enjoy a common loyalty with us, a common way of life and a common concept of democracy and loyalty to Her Majesty. We urged that some extra facility be granted to them by way of a somewhat less formal procedure, if you like, or some diminution of the obstacles placed in the way of their becoming Canadian citizens.
As I have said, the only thing that was done in that regard was in connection with the filing of a declaration of intention. There was that differentiation, in that British subjects were not required to file it. However, now that it is being abolished altogether there will be no mark of recognition whatsoever of the fact that an applicant for Canadian citizenship is already a British subject.
Therefore, while I cannot think of any amendment that would be in order at this stage, and would embody our thoughts so as to put them formally before the house by way of a resolution requiring a vote, I do strongly urge that the minister consider again what was urged in the past, that perhaps the time has now arrived-we think it is long past-when the waiting period for a British subject who is otherwise qualified might be shortened, as compared with the waiting period imposed upon those who do not share that common loyalty, that common concept of citizenship and, in short, do not share with us that family relationship that we like to think all subjects of Her Majesty in other parts of the commonwealth have. Now that this differentiation is being removed, I think it would be highly opportune

to bring in concurrent legislation to shorten the waiting period by at least one year, and I see no reason why in connection with British subjects it should not be shortened to a greater extent.
It is perhaps significant that this bill is being considered in the house immediately after a bill to provide diplomatic immunity for representatives from commonwealth countries, on which occasion we have been reminded of that common loyalty we share. In these days when international relationships are increasingly uneasy, anything we can do in this country to remind ourselves and people throughout the world that the British commonwealth of nations is a living and real concept, and that international brotherhood can and does exist, thus making a real contribution toward international good will and good faith, is worth doing. Not only that, but it would demonstrate in a real and practical way that we in Canada, the senior dominion of the commonwealth, are determined that so far as we are concerned this concept of a family relationship between countries of the commonwealth will be preserved and, indeed, strengthened.
It would be but a small gesture if we were to shorten the waiting period with respect to British subjects, and thus demonstrate our real loyalty to that concept. It would not do anything to make a differentiation between citizens, once they became citizens. That is not the idea at all. There would be no distinction between Canadian citizens, whatever their origin. But it would be a gesture which would mean something more than gestures usually mean, particularly in the light of the contribution that the commonwealth could make to international relations. If we were to take a firm stand it would mean that at least we in Canada are going to stand by that commonwealth and see that it means something in fact as well as in theory.

speechtext:
Does a person domiciled in Canada who is Canadian-born and desires to secure his Canadian citizenship certificate have to complete one type of application, while a British subject, who has come from the British Isles and has resided in Canada 83276-343
Canadian Citizenship Act for five years, has to complete another type of application? Is there a difference in the amount of fee paid in each case? If so, why?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL THE DECLARATION OF INTENTION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, replying to the last question, there is a difference in the form, but I understand the fee is the same in each case. The form of course in the first instance, where birth is in Canada, is accompanied by a birth certificate; the other recites birth in the British commonwealth.
Then, dealing with the question asked by the hon. member for Peterborough, I would say that the problem of identifying an alien who has become naturalized is dealt with in many different ways in many countries. As my hon. friend knows, we have been granting a certificate which is relatively large, thinking that it would be used only at home as part of a person's papers. From time to time, however, it is suggested that we ought to issue a smaller identification card which would certify that the holder has been granted citizenship. This would be convenient to carry around, especially in this country when one goes across the United States border. In that connection it is also suggested that we ought to have a picture of the naturalized person.
We have been examining the question of a smaller card for, I think, about three years. There are certain difficulties with which I need not trouble the committee; but it will fulfil the need I know in some cases, and if we find that we can do it without excessive cost I think we would. Under those conditions it would be desirable that there should be some identity attached to the card.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL THE DECLARATION OF INTENTION
speechtext: It was suggested by a United States immigration officer that even if the picture were on the back of a small card and the government stamp pushed through so that it could not be taken off it would be sufficient, and it would help them a great deal. They have those large certificates. If it were in a card form so that they would have a much easier time and less questioning of the Canadian citizen it would be an advantage. I might say that the citizenship branch here in Ottawa is certainly very co-operative and I feel they are doing a good job.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL THE DECLARATION OF INTENTION
speechtext: Will the minister say what was the reason in the first place that the declaration of intention was embodied in the statute? What was the reason that the institution of that requirement was made an obligatory course to be followed?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL THE DECLARATION OF INTENTION
speechtext: Initially, the declaration of intention followed the pattern of the United States system of having what is known as first papers, which would provide one with a certain status which would give him a claim upon the government of the country in which he lived. As I think hon. members know, in other days anyway if not lately, the taking out of first papers in the United States was considered something that one might very well do almost immediately. This would give him access to opportunities. That I think was the thought behind it, and we carried it forward in the original act with that in mind. We found that that was not necessary in Canada in a larger sense; but by way of explanation I should say that the regulations still provide for the filing of the declaration of intention, and will continue to do so despite the passage of this particular bill. So that if anyone feels that he would like to show anyone in Canada that he has already indicated by affidavit his desire to become a Canadian citizen, that opportunity will be open to him and the department will permit that to be done, believing that if it is in the interest of the applicant it might be granted.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL THE DECLARATION OF INTENTION
speechtext: What rights, if any, flow from the signing of a declaration of intention? Does it found any right to the protection of Canada in the way of a passport or anything of that kind?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL THE DECLARATION OF INTENTION

The rights and privileges which flow after a declaration and which have flowed in the past few years have been particularly that of being admitted to learned


societies and professional agencies so that one might compete in that particular field. Those organizations have indicated that they will accept the immigrant's application for membership if it were shown that he had filed a declaration of intention, and in that way he would not have to wait until he had received full citizenship. As I say, we are protecting that right under the regulations so that there is a direct benefit to certain persons in filing a declaration.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL THE DECLARATION OF INTENTION
speechtext: Will the minister also answer the rest of the question? Does the signing of the declaration of intention give any rights to passport protection?

speechtext: No. Until they become citizens they travel on the passports of their own home country.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL THE DECLARATION OF INTENTION
speechtext: Would the minister mind saying whether he sees any objection to the proposal that the waiting period with respect to British subjects might be somewhat reduced? I understand that Australia, for instance, insists on the full five years. I, however, would not accept that as an argument that we should do it because they do it. It might be a good thing if we were to set the pattern in this regard.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL THE DECLARATION OF INTENTION
speechtext: I have not studied the question lately, but it has been before us regularly since the citizenship act was passed. The reasons for not making a distinction, other than that mentioned by the hon. member earlier, were explained fully by the then secretary of state when he introduced the bill. I think on balance it is not desirable to have among those applying for citizenship any group that would have preferred treatment in the obtaining of it. While undoubtedly British subjects find it easier to qualify, nevertheless it would seem unusual if in a citizenship act you initially set up a class who would be preferred above others. After all, citizenship surely must be equal to all without distinction.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL THE DECLARATION OF INTENTION
speechtext:
With regard to what the minister has just said I wonder whether he might not reconsider this matter. The hon. member for Kamloops has presented the situation in his usual able manner and has covered the ground very thoroughly, but it is a matter of considerable importance.
I have always wondered why the British subject should have to undergo the same waiting period as anyone else coming to this country. I do not think that we want to make any distinction among immigrants, but the deferring of citizenship rights to a British subject is making a distinction unnecessarily

in the wrong quarter. There is, as the hon. member for Kamloops pointed out, the common background, the family background in the commonwealth of nations for those immigrants who come to us in large numbers from the United Kingdom and who are so welcomed.
There is the entire tradition of the British race behind them; there is the common language. The institutions are the same, and they fit so quickly and so readily into the Canadian life that it has always seemed to me to be an unnecessary restriction to impose that limitation of five years. I grant that there may be something said along that other angle that you are setting up a preference in favour of one group of immigrants rather than another, but more serious consideration should be given to this problem.
Our link with the United Kingdom and with members of the commonwealth is so strong that immigrants coming from the commonwealth should surely be received more quickly into Canadian citizenship than is set out according to the technical terms of this act. I think the act has floundered into a technicality and places unnecessary emphasis on this particular feature, and it has put our friends from the United Kingdom in a position in which they should not be placed.
After all, in view of what has been going on in this country over so many years, a country founded by two great races, but certainly receiving a great impetus from those who came from the United Kingdom, and in view of the fact that we did not impose any restrictions or restraint for generations, then I can see no reason why at this particular time, and during the past few years, we should have found means of making a distinction which was not observed in the past with regard to those who came to us from commonwealth countries, and particularly from the United Kingdom.
I think there is a great feeling on the part of the people of Canada that another look should be taken at this particular clause in the act and that it should be revised so that the immigrant coming to us from the British Isles is accepted much more readily and more quickly than is the case at the present time.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL THE DECLARATION OF INTENTION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rise to support the suggestion made by the hon. member for Peterborough to the effect that a small card showing Canadian citizenship and identification similar to the birth certificate issued by the province of Ontario 83276-343J
Canadian Citizenship Act should be issued to Canadian citizens so that it could be used for identification purposes any place in the world.
I would also like to support the suggestion made by the hon. member for Kamloops and the previous speaker to the effect that another look should be taken at the requirements of those coming from commonwealth countries whose tradition of democracy, common language and customs, should not be put in the same category as those who come from countries that are probably not used to our democratic way of life or schooled in our institutions. I think the minister should give the two suggestions very serious consideration.

Mr. Chairman, I certainly support the previous speaker, but I think they should go further in speaking of giving preferential treatment to citizens from other parts of the commonwealth. I think we should probably first concern ourselves with giving even equal treatment to citizens from different parts of the commonwealth.
In this connection I wonder if the minister is in a position to tell us what consideration has been given to a brief recently presented to him on behalf of coloured immigrants from the West Indies. These people often find it impossible to get into Canada much less become citizens when they do arrive here. Is the minister in a position to tell us anything about that situation?

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to engage in any discussion on immigration at this point. I am sure the hon. member is incorrect when he states that when they get in they cannot become citizens. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I find I have an explanation to make to the committee and an apology as well to certain hon. members. Yesterday there was delivered to me by the chief commissioner of the board of transport commissioners the original report on the railway grade crossing fund which matter had been under study by that board for some time. The chief commissioner of the board indicated to me that on May 17 the secretary of the board had delivered to my office a copy of that report, and I am sorry to have to say that I was not aware of this, although I should have been and I must take full responsibility for it. A copy of the report was sent to the translators by my officers and is being stencilled at the moment. During the discussion on my estimates the other day I rose when this matter was under discussion to say that the board had the railway grade crossing fund under study, and because of that I interrupted a number of hon. members, particularly the hon. member for Danforth. However, I think not too much harm followed because the hon. member and many other hon. members succeeded in getting onto Hansard what they intended to say. In any event, if they did not there is a particular item here in the estimates whereon they can discuss it at a later date. Meantime I want to apologize to the hon. member for Danforth and any other hon. members who were inconvenienced by reason of my stating that the grade crossing problem was under discussion and study by the board. At that time it was not under study by the board and I should have known so. I accept the full responsibility for that error.
I would like to add though that the report is a voluminous one, as hon. members can see. I have not had an opportunity to read it and neither have my colleagues, but I propose to ask their permission, when it is translated and stencilled, to table it and circulate copies to members before the end of the session. I do not think it will be possible to act on it at this late date.

I rise at this point to deal with certain matters in my own riding of Peel. Since the minister has mentioned the fact

that we have leave to discuss the matter of the grade crossing fund in its general aspect, I should like to avail myself of that opportunity at the present time to deal generally with that fund. It is statutory, and it is proper to deal with it at this time.
With respect to the first matter, I refer to the Malton airport. The minister will perhaps take satisfaction in hearing that we consider it to be one of the finest in the dominion. That is, of course, only proper since Peel is the finest county in the dominion. There is one matter that has arisen fairly recently that I should like to draw to the minister's attention, namely the proposed enlargement of the airport which has resulted in certain filings in the registry office of notices of expropriation and the like. These notices have caused considerable concern to land owners. The concern has been caused not so much by the actual filing of the notices as by the subsequent action resulting therefrom.
I am advised that after the notices were filed some negotiations took place and that subsequently some of the notices were withdrawn and the land use returned to the owners, with certain inconvenience to those owners. I would draw to the minister's attention the fact that that area is a fast developing one and that to turn back to the owners large tracts of land may well result in a rapid residential expansion which may well create a situation similar to that which was created recently around Downsview airport where representations were made by the residents with regard to nuisance and danger to their property and to themselves.
Another aspect of the expropriations is that which has arisen with respect to the owners of small holdings under the Veterans Land Act. There are a number of these owners. I am told that negotiations are going on and I suggest to the minister that he consider the advisability of expediting these negotiations so that the owners of these small holdings may know their immediate position rather quickly in order that they not be asked to expend further sums of money in completing their homes and then perhaps not receive the valuation which they themselves feel their holdings have. I would urge on the minister that this matter be completed rather quickly so that the people will not be left in a state of indecision, as are many of them at the present time.
With respect to the grade crossing fund, may I say that its history is perhaps of interest. I believe it was initiated about 1909, at which time 20 per cent of the total cost

of construction was advanced by the government for the elimination of grade crossings. Subsequently, in 1919, this advance was increased to 40 per cent, with no more than $25,000 to be expended on one work. In 1928 the government saw fit to increase the maximum for one work to $100,000. Then in 1950 an amendment provided for increasing the amount to $150,000.
In the county of Peel there are many grade crossings, some of which are active. When I say "active", I mean there are many trains crossing over them, as well as many automobiles and motor trucks. One in particular that has closely paralleled the amendments to the grade crossing fund-and when I say "paralleled" I mean the applications for some relief were made about the time of the amendments.
It is of interest to note the estimated cost of correcting the grade crossing in this one particular instance which is on the Canadian National Railways line from Toronto to Hamilton. It is perhaps one of the busiest stretches of railroad in the Dominion of Canada. In 1910 an application was first made and the estimated cost at that time was $21,000. In 1920 the matter was again reviewed and the estimated cost had risen to $73,000. Applications were again made in 1935, 1948 and 1952. At each of these latter applications, one of the objections raised was the increase in cost. A strong representation was made by the Canadian National Railways that while they did not object to the alleviation of the situation, they thought they should not be asked to pay any of the cost of this particular grade crossing.
The population in that area has increased in the few years since the war; it has doubled. According to the Canadian National Railways the rail travel is supposed to have decreased to some extent since about 1948. However, I would say that at the present time there would be in the neighbourhood of 125 trains travelling easterly along that track each day, and about the same number travelling westerly. In addition, there is a third track or a switching track. I would suggest to the minister that there would be in the neighbourhood of 100 switchings a day. Approximately 7,500 automobiles go over the crossing in a 24-hour period. The problem is a very real one.
The safety feature seems to have been taken care of there by the installation of signals and a gate and a watchman. Consider the time that is lost by travellers in motor cars making over 250 stops per day at that crossing in order to allow the watchman to lower the gates and to raise them. As to the
Supply-Transport
delay, if you take a minute for each crossing -which would be the minimum time, I would suggest-you would have a loss of time to a large number of motorists of over four hours in the 24 hours. I suggest to the minister that in such a busy area that is a considerable loss of time and therefore of money to those people.
There are other grade crossings in the south Peel area. There is one in particular which the Department of National Defence has perhaps assisted in making more dangerous. I refer to the one that is at the junction where the same Canadian National Railways line passes the road known as the first line or Cawthra road. It has taken the name "Cawthra" from a very old family that took the lands in that area by crown grant. The Department of National Defence have purchased part of those lands for a large ordnance warehouse.
This particular grade crossing is not level, as one would normally expect grade crossings to be, but rather has a very sharp incline of the road on the north rising at an angle of about 45 degrees and then a decline at the other side at about the same angle. There is an automatic signal at the crossing which I am told has been known not to work sometimes. I suggest that that is reasonable because on occasion automatic signals do not perform properly. Since the ordnance depot has been constructed there has been a considerable increase in the vehicular traffic over the crossing. It is a narrow crossing that is dangerous to pedestrians, and I suggest that its elimination really deserves the consideration of the government, particularly in view of the fact that the increased hazard has been created by another department of the government.
With respect to the grade crossing fund itself and the elimination of grade crossings generally, having in mind the report that the minister has in his hands, I suggest that some initiative should be taken by the government rather than the municipalities being put in the position of having to make an application each time and of being met with the constant opposition of a railway such as the Canadian National to expending money for the elimination of grade crossings which are dangerous and costly in that they result in a serious loss of time to people in built-up areas.
If the minister should have the pleasure some time of visiting our wonderful county I would invite him to inspect the crossings on Hurontario street. At any time of the day he will see long lines of vehicles waiting to cross this main line of the Canadian

Supply-Transport
National Railways. In many instances I have seen a line of waiting vehicles a mile long. Much time is lost there by people who are busy and the dollars represented by time lost by Canadian citizens would eventually pay for the elimination of that level crossing.
Having regard to the history of applications to have the level crossing eliminated, I suggest to the minister that other steps must be taken in these cases to bring about the elimination of such problems. When people have applied over a period of some forty-two years for the elimination of this crossing their application must have some merit. It is not a case of someone suddenly getting the idea of applying for the elimination of a crossing. There is a history of applications for the elimination of this crossing over a period of forty-two years, but in all instances the board has not granted the request because of the resistance of the railway involved to paying its proper share. I suggest to the minister that consideration might well be given, where it is in the interests of commerce and the travelling public as a whole, to taking the initiative in eliminating such crossings rather than leaving it to the municipalities involved to make application.
There is one further point I should like to make with respect to this line of the Canadian National Railways. A commuter service is provided, and while in the past it may have been adequate I suggest with the increased population in the area and the large number of commuters who live there and work in the city of Toronto serious consideration should be given to improving the service offered both with respect to the number of trains and the type of equipment. I suggest to the minister that having regard to the size of the city of Toronto and the population in the immediate area through which the commuter trains travel the service provided does not compare with that provided for any other city on the North American continent. It seems to be an area that has been forgotten so far as commuter service is concerned. I draw that matter to the minister's attention because I know that having been brought to his attention he will see to it that, in the best interests of the people concerned, some action is taken.

I wish to refer to railway crossings in the city of White Rock. White Rock has British Columbia's safest beach in many respects, and it certainly is one of the finest. Practically every Sunday between 20,000 and
30,000	people go there. However, between Washington avenue in the city itself and the beach there is the Great Northern Railway

line. Prior to 1951 there were two crossings from the main street in the city over the railroad to the beach. In 1951 the Great Northern Railway saw fit to change the track and close the crossings. As you can well imagine there was an immediate effect upon the tourist traffic to such a notable area as this beach. The people concerned have made requests on more than one occasion that the railroad crossings be placed there again so that traffic can get to the beach, thus facilitating use of the beach. The Minister of Transport was sent a letter on January 16 of this year embodying that request, and I was wondering whether or not he would like to answer it at this time.

I am not going to take very long, but I think this is the proper place to bring up this matter. It has to do with the Railway Act, and I believe that the only way that the situation can be rectified is to amend the act. I bring this matter to the minister's attention because it is not so long ago that, rightly or wrongly, I headed off a bunch of petitions that were going to be sent to him with respect to overpasses and underpasses. Under section 265 of the Railway Act I understand that the board of transport commissioners does not consider that these are railway crossings towards which a contribution may be made for the elimination of danger when applications are made by municipal authorities for elimination or widening of underpasses or overpasses.
There is a serious situation in my constituency, and I call it an underpass because the highway goes under the railroad. It was built in the days when there was nothing on the road but the horse and wagon, and it was quite safe then. Now, the highway has been widened on both sides of the railroad, and the underpass is at an angle of, I would say, nearly 45 degrees to the highway. This means that any traffic coming up from the south towards the underpass cannot see the traffic approaching on the other side. I believe the act should be changed so that a portion of the money allotted for the improvement of crossings should be applicable to underpasses. Since there is no authority to do that, there is not much use saying any more.
I believe there are two other dangerous crossings in the province of New Brunswick, and I believe they are underpasses, at which several people have been killed in the past few years. I know the one in the county of Victoria is very dangerous, and we would like

to have the minister consider this matter to see whether next year there might be some amendment introduced to the act.

speechtext: I can give an interim answer now but it would not add, I am sorry to say, a great deal more to what was said by the Minister of Trade and Commerce earlier. I should like to take a
moment or two to express my appreciation to the minister, and through him to the board of transport commissioners, for the expeditious manner in which the request for a hearing on the Canadian National St. George street railway crossing was dealt with last January. May I also express my appreciation to the hon. member for Middlesex East, who so capably looked after the interests of the constituents of Elgin in this matter.
The railway crossing to which I have referred is on the outskirts of the city of St. Thomas and is located on the brow of a very steep hill. The grade is as high as 16 per cent. I refer specifically to this crossing as one of the many crossings in the county of Elgin. It was in the interests of the travelling public that prior to his sudden death the late C. D. Coyle, who was for many years a member of this house, endeavoured to secure added protection and had made the appointment for the hearing by the board of transport commissioners to which I made reference a few moments ago.
As you drive along the highways of rural Canada you find many crossings with practically no protection except the crossing sign. In fact, in Canada there are 25,000 of these crossings. Only 6-2 per cent of rural crossings in Canada have protective devices, and where those are to be found the most usual type of automatic signal is the flashing lights or bells. Subways and bridges offer complete protection, but there are not many of them. There are subways at only 2 per cent of all rural crossings, and bridges at 1-4 per cent. A few crossings have manually operated

Supply-Transport
gates and a very few have a watchman. This type of protection is scarce because of the high cost of labour.
In the towns and cities nearly 30 per cent of the railway crossings are protected, and the devices used are usually the same as those in the rural areas. Actually, the number of protected crossings, both rural and urban, has kept pace with the increased number of crossings. In the last 30 years some 5,000 new crossings have been added to the total. The main reason why there is not complete protection at every crossing is financial.
Ten o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I hear some hon. members calling ten o'clock. I am sure that if the hon. member has only a few remarks to make hon. members will bear with him for a few minutes.
I shall be very brief.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Has the hon. member unanimous consent to continue?
Agreed.

While there are now over
32,000	crossings in Canada, the number injured and killed was three times greater in 1950 than in 1920. Since 1920 more deaths and injuries have occurred at rural crossings than urban crossings, and the reverse was the case before 1920. The rapid increase in the number of automobiles has been mainly responsible for this situation. There are over six times as many automobiles on the roads now as there were in 1921. In addition, the greater speed of highway traffic and the increase in the amount of traffic offer extra hazards. As I stated before, only 6-2 per cent of the rural crossings have any protective devices.
In 1950 the number of people killed at rural crossings was 87, and there were 224 injured. There has however been a decrease in the number of accidents in rural areas since 1947, when there were 101 deaths and 306 injured. This may indicate the effectiveness of some of the improvements made at level crossings.
The matter of solving the level crossing problem is not as simple as one might think. It involves the matter of finance, how to divide the cost and how to spend the available money. What kind of protection is needed at railway crossings to prevent accidents? The only sure protection is a bridge or subway. By separating the highway from the railway an overhead bridge or subway does away with level crossings and eliminates the danger of a crash.
Then, how effective are the flashing lights, bells and other automatic devices? I understand the board of transport commissioners made a survey of over 1,000 crossings as a check on the kinds of protection and the number of accidents. The results were as follows: Subways and overhead bridges; no accidents. Manually operated gates; some accidents at city and town streets, and provincial highways. Automatic signals, many accidents at city and town streets, some on provincial highways and a few on rural roads. Unprotected; the greatest number of accidents on all kinds of roads, whether urban, rural or provincial highways.
Thus the evidence indicates that automatic signals offer a fair measure of protection on rural roads. On city streets, however, it appears that the traffic is so heavy as to limit the effectiveness of lights and bells. On provincial highways they are also less effective than on secondary country roads. Many of the new provincial highways have no railway crossings at all, as overhead bridge or subways were built as part of the highway scheme.
I do not propose taking up further time, but I would say to the minister that progress is being made on the St. George street crossing to which I referred. I hope we will have the continued support of the minister on that project.
